topic: What are the limits of heat transfer in matter? Materials science research may help address high-power-density heat-transfer challenges across length scales, from nanometre-scale electronic devices and circuits to industrial-scale processes such as power plants. The research focus is to identify fundamental and material-dependent limits on thermal transport, interfacial thermal resistance, phonon and electron heat conduction, and heat dissipation under high power density.

mature_ideas.title: Operational Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures Under High-Power-Density Thermal Cycling
mature_ideas.hypothesis: Random interlayer rotations engineered to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: Random interlayer rotations engineered to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape.
mature_ideas.scientific_object: Twisted multilayer van der Waals heterostructures (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) with controlled interlayer rotation angles
mature_ideas.mechanism: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder

mature_ideas.title: Dynamic Twist Angle Tuning via Strain-Mediated Moiré Potential Modulation
mature_ideas.hypothesis: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: Instead of relying on static twist angles, dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via applied mechanical strain can actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity in real-time, enabling adaptive thermal management that responds to operational heat flux demands.
mature_ideas.mechanism: Apply controlled biaxial strain to twisted van der Waals heterostructures while measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity. Use piezoelectric actuators or thermal expansion mismatch to modulate strain dynamically. Correlate strain-induced moiré potential changes with thermal conductivity variations. This tests whether twist-angle engineering can be made adaptive rather than static.

mature_ideas.title: Quantitative Crossover Boundary from Bulk-Dominated to Interface-Dominated Thermal Resistance in Heterogeneous Interfaces Under High Power Density
mature_ideas.hypothesis: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable critical interface bonding energy threshold that scales with the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length, and this threshold shifts under high-power-density conditions due to non-equilibrium phonon population effects.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance occurs at a predictable critical interface bonding energy threshold that scales with the ratio of bulk phonon mean free path to interface characteristic length, and this threshold shifts under high-power-density conditions due to non-equilibrium phonon population effects.
mature_ideas.scientific_object: Heterogeneous material interfaces (metal-semiconductor, dielectric-substrate, van der Waals junctions) with systematically varied bonding strength and contamination levels
mature_ideas.mechanism: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

mature_ideas.title: Discriminating Observation Protocol for Partitioning Phonon vs. Electron Heat Conduction Contributions in High-Power-Density Materials
mature_ideas.hypothesis: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials can be discriminated by exploiting the differential response of each carrier type to controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, combined with spectral phonon imaging to directly visualize phonon transport pathways.
mature_ideas.central_hypothesis: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials can be discriminated by exploiting the differential response of each carrier type to controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, combined with spectral phonon imaging to directly visualize phonon transport pathways.
mature_ideas.scientific_object: High-power-density materials (wide-bandgap semiconductors, doped thermoelectrics, metallic thin films) under controlled carrier density and temperature gradients
mature_ideas.mechanism: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
mature_ideas.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
assumptions: Wiedemann-Franz law deviations can be attributed primarily to electron-phonon coupling rather than other scattering mechanisms
Spectral phonon imaging has sufficient resolution to distinguish phonon contributions from electron contributions
Carrier density variations do not significantly alter phonon dispersion or scattering rates
The material system allows independent control of carrier density without introducing additional defect scattering

SURVEY_ANCHOR: 'What evidence distinguishes the relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to the maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials?'
SURVEY_ANCHOR: 'No discriminating observation differentiates phonon-mediated from electron-mediated heat conduction contributions under comparable high-power-density conditions'
mature_ideas.refinement_scope: Develop and validate a discriminating observation protocol that can partition phonon and electron heat conduction contributions under high-power-density conditions, addressing the identifiability gap in the survey
mature_ideas.falsifier: Demonstration that phonon and electron contributions cannot be independently varied or measured with sufficient precision to distinguish their relative contributions, or that Wiedemann-Franz deviations are dominated by mechanisms other than electron-phonon coupling

representative.title: Spectral Thermal Boundary Conductance Calibration via Phonon Spectroscopy Feedback in van der Waals Heterostructures
representative.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet kinetic transport models rely on static boundary assumptions that fail to predict when interface resistance overtakes bulk resistance. We replace the static Kapitza resistance assumption with a dynamically calibrated spectral thermal boundary conductance, driven by iterative model-experiment calibration using mean-free-path-resolving phonon spectroscopy in dielectric-dielectric systems. By closing the loop between time-domain thermoreflectance measurements and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation via inverse modeling, we establish the exact physical and power-density thresholds where interfacial resistance dominates, explicitly decoupling phonon spectral mismatch from electron-phonon and defect-scattering confounders. This mechanism-commit innovation resolves the unmapped boundary variable gap, enabling predictive thermal design for high-power-density electronics.
representative.core_contribution: Replacing the static boundary assumption in kinetic transport models with a dynamically calibrated spectral thermal boundary conductance in dielectric-dielectric van der Waals heterostructures, iteratively refined via inverse modeling of phonon spectroscopy data to define the precise power-density threshold where interfacial thermal resistance overtakes bulk thermal resistance, while isolating the signal from electron-phonon and defect-scattering confounders.
representative.method:
Conceptual Move: Replace the static boundary assumption in kinetic transport modeling with a dynamic, closed-loop calibration driven by experimental phonon spectroscopy characterization.

Step 1 (Rewire phonon_spectroscopy_characterization -> interfacial_boundary_variable): Use time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) and frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) with variable modulation frequencies to measure phonon group velocities, mode-specific scattering rates, and spectral transmission at the van der Waals heterostructure interface. Feed these measurements into a bounded delta update rule that iteratively adjusts the spectral thermal boundary conductance (the interfacial_boundary_variable) in the phonon Boltzmann transport equation. Require corroboration across multiple spectral windows before updating Kapitza resistance parameters.

Step 2 (bulk_conduction_ablation protocol): Disable the interfacial feedback loop and assume bulk-dominated Fourier transport with a fixed, literature-value boundary condition. Compare the predicted total thermal resistance against the closed-loop calibrated model to isolate the contribution of the dynamically calibrated boundary variable to overall thermal resistance.

Step 3 (high_power_density_stress protocol): Subject the heterostructure to progressively increasing power densities while monitoring feedback loop convergence. Record the power-density threshold where non-equilibrium hot optical phonon populations cause the calibrated boundary variable to diverge, explicitly defining the model's validity boundary.
representative.risks:
Risk 1: Phonon spectroscopy (TDTR/FDTR) may suffer from spatial averaging that convolves bulk and interfacial scattering, corrupting the inverse modeling signal. Mitigation: Use frequency-domain thermoreflectance with variable modulation frequencies to selectively probe different thermal penetration depths, isolating the interfacial contribution from bulk phonon scattering.

Risk 2: High power density stress may induce non-linear phonon-phonon scattering (three-phonon Umklapp processes) that breaks the linear boundary conductance assumption. Mitigation: Explicitly bound the model's validity to the regime where hot optical phonon populations remain below the threshold for dominant non-equilibrium effects, and record this threshold as a measurable failure boundary.

Risk 3: Interfacial defects or impurities could mimic spectral mismatch. Mitigation: Restrict the material system to high-quality dielectric-dielectric van der Waals interfaces and use structural characterization (e.g., STEM) to bound the defect density, ensuring defect-scattering does not confound the phonon spectroscopy signal.
representative.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped_gap:boundary_variable by transforming a static, poorly-defined boundary condition into a dynamically calibrated variable grounded in experimental phonon spectroscopy. By committing to a single mechanism surface—the spectral thermal boundary conductance—and replacing the weak static assumption with a refined dynamic calibration, the research shifts from descriptive reviews to predictive modeling of the exact power-density threshold where interface resistance dominates. The ablation protocol rigorously isolates the mechanism's contribution.

mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

representative.title: Moiré Potential Landscapes Dictate the Thermal Cycling Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
representative.abstract: Engineered interlayer twist angles suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures, but their stability under operational thermal cycling remains unverified across diverse materials. We replace the complex shear-strain locking mechanism with a fundamental boundary condition governed by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape. We demonstrate that engineered twist angles remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, and in the absence of confounding defect-mediated or chemically-induced pinning. By synthesizing heterostructures across diverse material families and subjecting them to controlled thermal cycling, we isolate the moiré potential mechanism and establish the material-dependent limits of thermal anisotropy retention.
representative.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy under operational thermal cycling is strictly bounded by a critical interlayer binding energy threshold dictated by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, specifically in regimes where defect-mediated and chemically-induced interlayer pinning are negligible.
representative.method: We conceptualize the stability of random interlayer rotations not through complex interlayer shear-strain locking feedback loops, but through the fundamental energy barriers of the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape. We synthesize a library of van der Waals heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2, graphene/hBN) with controlled random interlayer rotations. We subject these structures to sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients. We then characterize the cross-plane thermal conductivity before and after cycling. By comparing the thermal anisotropy retention across materials with varying moiré potential depths, we perform a material-dependent binding energy ablation to isolate the moiré potential mechanism and confirm the critical energy threshold for structural stability.
representative.risks: Primary risk is that thermal cycling could induce interlayer diffusion or chemical bonding (e.g., via chalcogen vacancies) that pins the layers, providing an alternative explanation for the retention of thermal anisotropy independent of moiré potential pinning. Mitigation involves using low-temperature cycling regimes and verifying structural integrity via cross-sectional TEM to rule out chemical bridging. Secondary risk is that thermal contact resistance changes during cycling could mimic changes in intrinsic cross-plane thermal conductivity. Mitigation involves using suspended membrane geometries and time-domain thermoreflectance to decouple contact resistance from intrinsic material properties.
representative.rationale: This skill application resolves the missing assumption of structural stability and the material generality boundary condition by replacing the parent's complex shear-strain locking mechanism with a fundamental, material-dependent moiré potential energy threshold. It sharpens the parent idea's thesis by grounding the operational stability of thermal anisotropy in a clear, falsifiable physical mechanism that naturally extends across diverse van der Waals material families.

mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Thermal resistance in heterogeneous systems is partitioned between bulk phonon scattering (governed by Umklapp and Normal processes) and interfacial Kapitza resistance (governed by acoustic mismatch and bonding topology). The crossover point where interface resistance dominates bulk resistance depends on: (1) the bulk phonon mean free path distribution relative to device dimensions, (2) the interface transmission probability determined by bonding strength and chemical compatibility, and (3) non-equilibrium phonon populations under high heat flux that alter effective scattering rates. When interface bonding energy falls below a critical threshold, Kapitza resistance becomes the rate-limiting step regardless of bulk material quality.

representative.title: Flux-Dependent Spectral Transmission Threshold for the Bulk-to-Interface Thermal Resistance Crossover
representative.abstract: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance is traditionally modeled using static acoustic mismatch or equilibrium bonding energy thresholds. We propose a representation shift: defining the critical crossover boundary through the flux-dependent spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations. By modulating interface bonding energy and applying high-power-density heat flux, we demonstrate that the critical threshold shifts predictably as hot phonons alter the effective transmission probability via anharmonic interactions. This non-equilibrium spectral transmission model resolves the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit for weakly bonded interfaces and identifies the precise boundary variable governing the crossover under operational conditions, explicitly decoupled from local thermal expansion and equilibrium bulk scattering artifacts.
representative.core_contribution: The critical interface bonding energy threshold for the bulk-to-interface thermal resistance crossover is not a static material constant, but a flux-dependent parameter defined by the spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations, shifting the validity boundary of the maximum transmission limit under high power density independent of equilibrium thermal expansion.
representative.method: Conceptual move: Shift the representation of the interface boundary from a static acoustic mismatch threshold to a flux-dependent spectral transmission threshold. Methodology: 1) Synthesize phononic_interface_systems (e.g., Si/Ge heterostructures) with systematically varied interface_bonding_energy_modulation via controlled surface functionalization. 2) Rewire the experimental loop such that ultrafast_spectral_phonon_characterization directly informs iterative interface_bonding_energy_modulation to pinpoint the crossover boundary. 3) Perform isotopic_mean_free_path_ablation using isotopically pure vs. natural materials to decouple bulk phonon mean free path from interface scattering. 4) Apply high_power_density_heat_flux_stress to stress test the feedback loop, confirming the shifted boundary condition and recording failure boundaries where irreversible interface reconstruction occurs.
representative.risks: ['Risk 1: High-power-density measurements may induce local thermal expansion or irreversible interface reconstruction, masking the non-equilibrium phonon effect. Mitigation: Use ultrafast pulsed heating with low duty cycles and mechanically constrain the interface.', 'Risk 2: Isotopic ablation might introduce unintended interface defects. Mitigation: Rigorous TEM and XPS characterization.', 'Risk 3: The observed threshold shift may be conflated with bulk thermal conductivity changes. Mitigation: Use isotopic ablation to decouple bulk mean free path effects.']
representative.rationale: This representation shift resolves the unmapped boundary variable by explicitly defining the crossover threshold in terms of non-equilibrium phonon spectral overlap, rather than static bonding energy. It addresses the missing boundary condition by delineating the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit for non-ideal interfaces under high flux, directly repairing the parent idea's scope without altering its core thesis.

representative.title: Direct Observation of Saturating Interfacial Thermal Conductance in Annealed Graphene/SiO2 Heterostructures Reveals Bonding-Dependent Phonon Transmission Limits
representative.abstract: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance fundamentally limits heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing thermal conductance saturation remain unobserved. We demonstrate that interfacial thermal conductance in graphene/SiO2 heterostructures saturates at a critical covalent bond density, revealing a fundamental limit to phonon transmission enhancement through interface engineering. Using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy, we directly observe non-monotonic thermal conductance evolution during controlled annealing, where initial van der Waals-to-covalent bonding transitions increase conductance, but excessive covalent bonding introduces defect scattering that degrades heat transfer. This discriminating observation falsifies monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a bonding-configuration-dependent upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.
representative.core_contribution: Interfacial thermal conductance exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on covalent bond density, saturating and then degrading due to competing phonon transmission enhancement and defect scattering mechanisms, establishing a fundamental material-dependent limit on thermal transport across engineered interfaces.
representative.method: We synthesize graphene/SiO2 van der Waals heterostructures via chemical vapor deposition and dry transfer to create atomically sharp interfaces. We apply controlled thermal annealing (200-600°C in vacuum) to systematically tune interfacial bonding from pure van der Waals to mixed van der Waals-covalent to defect-rich covalent configurations. We characterize the atomic bonding configuration using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy to quantify covalent bond density (C-O-Si bridge bonds) and defect concentration. We measure interfacial thermal conductance using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy with <10 ps temporal resolution across the annealing series. We ablate the mechanism by comparing as-grown van der Waals interfaces, optimally annealed interfaces at peak conductance, and over-annealed defect-rich interfaces to isolate bonding configuration effects from bulk property changes, directly observing the saturation and degradation of thermal conductance.
representative.risks: Risk 1: Annealing may cause graphene degradation rather than controlled interface modification. Mitigation: Use Raman spectroscopy to monitor graphene quality (2D/G ratio) and limit annealing temperature to <600°C where graphene remains intact. Risk 2: Thermal conductance changes may be dominated by bulk SiO2 property changes rather than interface effects. Mitigation: Use thickness-controlled SiO2 samples (>100 nm) and compare with bulk SiO2 thermal conductivity measurements to isolate interface contribution. Risk 3: Ultrafast thermoreflectance may not achieve sufficient sensitivity for sub-nm interface layers. Mitigation: Use high-repetition-rate laser system (80 MHz) and lock-in detection with signal averaging to achieve <1% measurement uncertainty on thermal decay time constants.
representative.rationale: This skill application resolves the direct_observation gap by providing direct experimental observation of thermal conductance saturation at atomic-scale interfaces under controlled bonding configurations. The verification reversal route ensures the mechanism is back-inferred from observable thermal transport limits rather than assumed a priori. The non-monotonic conductance dependence serves as a pre-registered discriminating outcome that falsifies simple monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a fundamental upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.

representative.title: Commensurability-Mediated Covalent Phonon Bridging in van der Waals Heterostructures for High-Power-Density Thermal Dissipation
representative.abstract: The fundamental limit of heat transfer across van der Waals interfaces is conventionally attributed to weak interfacial coupling and diffuse phonon scattering. We invert this premise by demonstrating that covalent interfacial functionalization does not universally enhance thermal boundary conductance; rather, it acts as a commensurability-mediated phonon bridge. By precisely controlling the interfacial atomic registry via twist-angle alignment in graphene/hexagonal boron nitride heterostructures, we show that covalent functionalization yields a massive thermal boundary conductance spike only in commensurate (aligned) registries with minimized moiré strain, while acting as a scattering sink in incommensurate ones. Using time-domain thermoreflectance, we bound the maximum heat flux limits under high power density, revealing that atomic alignment dictates the efficacy of covalent thermal bridging, provided intralayer defect scattering is minimized and twist-angle-dependent electron-phonon coupling variations are decoupled.
representative.core_contribution: The thermal boundary conductance enhancement via covalent interfacial functionalization is strictly dependent on the interfacial atomic registry and minimized moiré strain, establishing commensurability as the fundamental structural invariant for overcoming van der Waals thermal bottlenecks, contingent on sub-percolation defect densities and decoupled from twist-angle-dependent electron-phonon coupling.
representative.method: The conceptual move replaces the assumption of universal weak van der Waals scattering with a commensurability-mediated covalent phonon bridging mechanism. We synthesize van der Waals heterostructures (graphene/hBN) with controlled twist angles (0° commensurate and 30° incommensurate) using deterministic dry transfer to tune the interfacial atomic registry. We then apply covalent interfacial functionalization via diazonium grafting at ultra-low density (<0.1% coverage) to modulate bonding strength while preserving intralayer transport. We characterize the thermal boundary conductance using time-domain thermoreflectance under high-power-density pumping (up to 10 GW/m²). We perform a twist-angle moiré ablation, comparing the thermal response of commensurate (0°) versus incommensurate (30°) registries to isolate the registry-dependent effect. Local Raman mapping and in situ Raman thermometry verify registry preservation and detect structural degradation thresholds.
representative.risks: ['1) Diazonium grafting may introduce excessive point defects in the graphene lattice, degrading intrinsic in-plane thermal conductivity and masking interfacial gains. Mitigation: use ultra-low-density functionalization (<0.1% coverage).', '2) High-power-density pumping in time-domain thermoreflectance may induce irreversible interfacial delamination. Mitigation: employ in situ Raman thermometry to detect structural degradation thresholds.', '3) The interfacial twist angle may relax or shift during chemical functionalization, inducing moiré strain. Mitigation: use deterministic dry transfer with edge-clamping and verify via Raman.', '4) Local structural relaxation around covalent bonds in incommensurate interfaces might create localized commensurate patches, artificially inflating the incommensurate thermal conductance. Mitigation: high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to verify the absence of local relaxation.', '5) Twist-angle-dependent variations in electron-phonon coupling could confound the purely phononic bridging mechanism. Mitigation: utilize pump-probe techniques with varying excitation wavelengths to decouple electronic and phononic contributions.']
representative.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped target_object gap by explicitly defining the van der Waals heterostructure as the nanoscale electronic material system and its interfacial atomic registry as the structural state under high power density. It sharpens the parent idea by moving from a generic 'covalent bonding improves heat transfer' assumption to a precise, falsifiable mechanism where atomic commensurability is the required invariant for thermal bridging. The twist-angle moiré ablation provides a minimal validation suite that directly falsifies the core mechanism.

representative.claim_scope: Applies to van der Waals heterostructures (graphene/hBN) with controlled twist angles under high-power-density thermal loading, strictly conditioned on the functionalization density remaining below the intralayer defect percolation threshold, the minimization of moiré-induced strain fields, and the absence of local relaxation-induced nanoscale commensurability; excludes regimes where twist-angle-dependent electron-phonon coupling dominates.
representative.falsifier: A result showing a significant thermal boundary conductance enhancement in incommensurate (30°) functionalized interfaces that cannot be attributed to local structural relaxation, moiré strain, or measurement artifacts, or a result showing the commensurate enhancement fails despite sub-percolation defect densities and minimal strain, or evidence that twist-angle-dependent electron-phonon coupling fully accounts for the conductance differences.

representatives.direction_summary: Favor cross-domain transfer: reusing strong ideas from domain A in domain B, with less emphasis on raw novelty and more on fit. Emphasize the transferable principle of stability-bounded structural modulation to ensure measurement validity in adaptive thermal management.
representatives.title: Stability-Bounded Dynamic Moiré Potential Modulation for Adaptive Cross-Plane Thermal Conductivity
representatives.abstract: Dynamic modulation of the moiré potential via mechanical strain offers a pathway to actively tune interfacial thermal conductance and effective cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted van der Waals heterostructures. However, measurement constructs often conflate true moiré-mediated thermal transport changes with structural degradation, such as twist-angle relaxation, or with intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts in the individual layers. We introduce a stability-bounded strain perturbation protocol that restricts dynamic moiré modulation to regimes where the strain energy remains below the interlayer binding energy barrier, preventing twist-angle relaxation. By correlating in situ electron diffraction with cross-plane thermal conductivity during thermal cycling, and comparing against untwisted control heterostructures, we isolate the pure moiré potential contribution from intrinsic bulk phonon shifts. This approach validates the structural stability assumption and extends the adaptive thermal management paradigm from MoS2/WS2 to broader transition metal dichalcogenides.
representatives.core_contribution: The establishment of a critical-strain-bounded structural stability condition for strain-mediated moiré potential modulation, ensuring that measured variations in interfacial thermal conductance and effective cross-plane thermal conductivity strictly reflect dynamic moiré landscape alterations rather than irreversible twist-angle relaxation or intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts.
representatives.central_hypothesis: Strain-mediated modulation of the moiré potential can dynamically tune interfacial thermal conductance—and thereby the effective cross-plane thermal conductivity of thin heterostructures—by >20%, provided the applied strain remains below the critical strain threshold dictated by the interlayer binding energy barrier, and the contribution from intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts is bounded or subtracted.
representatives.mechanism_or_relation: Strain-induced moiré potential modulation alters local interlayer stacking registry and cross-plane phonon transport pathways across the van der Waals gap, bounded by the critical strain threshold required to maintain twist-angle structural stability, distinct from intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts within the individual layers.
representatives.expected_mechanism: Strain alters the moiré superlattice periodicity and local registry (e.g., AA to AB stacking transitions), modifying the interfacial phonon transmission and scattering rates across the van der Waals gap, thereby tuning interfacial thermal conductance without altering the fundamental macroscopic twist angle, while intrinsic out-of-plane phonon dispersion shifts in the individual layers are bounded or accounted for.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Interfacial thermal conductance and effective cross-plane thermal conductivity changes correlate linearly with strain-induced moiré potential shifts measured via ultrafast electron diffraction in twisted heterostructures, but remain invariant in untwisted control heterostructures subjected to the same strain, confirming the effect is moiré-mediated rather than due to intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts or contact resistance changes.
representatives.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails or becomes unsafe when the applied strain exceeds the critical strain threshold, causing irreversible twist-angle relaxation, interfacial sliding, or microcracking, which decouples the thermal conductivity from the moiré potential, or when the layer thickness is too large, causing bulk thermal resistance to dominate over interfacial resistance.
representatives.claim_scope: Valid for twisted transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures with layer thicknesses ensuring interfacial thermal resistance dominates bulk layer resistance, under biaxial strain up to 2% and thermal cycling within the stability bound, specifically addressing effective cross-plane thermal conductivity where moiré-mediated interfacial scattering is the primary variable.
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy is sufficient to prevent twist-angle relaxation up to the critical strain threshold.
The heterostructure layer thickness is sufficiently small that interfacial thermal resistance dominates intrinsic bulk layer thermal resistance.
Strain-induced changes in the intrinsic out-of-plane phonon dispersion of the individual TMD layers are either negligible or can be explicitly subtracted using untwisted control heterostructures.
representatives.gap_alignment: Addresses the fundamental limits of thermal transport and interfacial thermal resistance by establishing a material-dependent stability boundary for dynamic moiré-mediated heat dissipation under high power density, while rigorously decoupling interfacial effects from bulk phonon shifts.
representatives.evidence_requirement: Correlated measurements of strain-dependent moiré potential and local registry via diffraction, interfacial thermal conductance and effective cross-plane thermal conductivity via thermoreflectance in both twisted and untwisted heterostructures, and twist-angle distribution before and after thermal cycling to distinguish moiré-mediated transport from structural degradation and bulk phonon shifts.
representatives.evidence_basis: Molecular dynamics predictions of critical strain thresholds, moiré-dependent interfacial thermal conductance, and intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts, validated against experimental electron diffraction and time-domain thermoreflectance measurements.
representatives.falsifier: Measure effective cross-plane thermal conductivity and interfacial thermal conductance as a function of applied strain (0-2% biaxial) in both twisted and untwisted MoS2 heterostructures. Use ultrafast X-ray diffraction to track moiré pattern and registry changes. If the thermal conductivity tuning in the twisted heterostructure is not significantly greater than in the untwisted control, or if changes correlate primarily with intrinsic phonon dispersion shifts rather than moiré registry changes, the hypothesis is falsified.
representatives.risks: Primary risk is that the critical strain threshold is too low for any measurable thermal modulation, or that intrinsic bulk phonon shifts are too large to be effectively subtracted via controls. Mitigation involves using molecular dynamics to pre-screen transition metal dichalcogenide combinations with higher interlayer binding energies and employing ultra-thin layers to ensure interface-dominated transport.

representatives.title: Time-Temperature-Transformation Stability Boundaries for Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in van der Waals Heterostructures
representatives.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in van der Waals heterostructures assumes structural stability under high-power-density operation, yet single-point thermal validations fail to capture time-dependent relaxation and often conflate it with defect-mediated phonon scattering or interfacial delamination. We introduce a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) stability boundary for twist angles, mapping the critical temperature-time combinations where the interfacial twist angle remains preserved versus relaxes. By replacing single-point thermal validation with a continuous stability phase diagram, we establish a predictive framework for the operational limits of twist-angle-engineered heat dissipation. We validate this boundary by correlating cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation with electron diffraction quantification of twist angle relaxation across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides, while explicitly decoupling these effects from thermally generated point defects and interfacial delamination using Raman spectroscopy and cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy, bounded by molecular dynamics-derived critical binding energy thresholds.
representatives.core_contribution: We replace the single-point thermal validation of twist-angle stability with a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) stability boundary, providing a predictive phase diagram that discriminates between preserved and relaxed interfacial twist angles under high-power-density thermal loads. This resolves the measurement construct mismatch in twist-angle-engineered thermal transport by explicitly decoupling true twist angle relaxation from confounding mechanisms such as point defect generation and interfacial delamination.
representatives.central_hypothesis: The structural stability of interfacial twist angles in van der Waals heterostructures under high-power-density thermal loads is governed by a time-temperature-transformation boundary, such that the twist angle relaxes only when specific critical temperature-time combinations are exceeded, and this relaxation is the dominant mechanism for thermal conductivity degradation, distinct from and sub-dominant to defect-mediated phonon scattering and interfacial delamination within the defined operational window.
representatives.mechanism_or_relation: thermal_relaxation_mechanism governing the thermally activated, time-dependent structural relaxation of the twist angle at the van der Waals interface, distinct from defect-mediated phonon scattering and interfacial delamination.
representatives.expected_mechanism: The thermal_relaxation_mechanism is thermally activated and time-dependent, meaning that the interfacial van der Waals binding energy is overcome over time at elevated temperatures, causing the twist angle to relax and degrading the engineered thermal anisotropy, while point defect generation and delamination follow distinct, separable kinetic pathways.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Quantification of the twist_angle_relaxation_state via nanobeam electron diffraction and cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements across a matrix of isothermal holds, compared against the stability_phase_diagram boundary, while simultaneously tracking defect density via Raman spectroscopy and interfacial integrity via cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy to rule out competing mechanisms.

representatives.title: Flux-Dependent Spectral Transmission Threshold for the Bulk-to-Interface Thermal Resistance Crossover
representatives.abstract: The transition from bulk-dominated to interface-dominated thermal resistance is traditionally modeled using static acoustic mismatch or equilibrium bonding energy thresholds. We propose a representation shift: defining the critical crossover boundary through the flux-dependent spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations. By modulating interface bonding energy and applying high-power-density heat flux, we demonstrate that the critical threshold shifts predictably as hot phonons alter the effective transmission probability via anharmonic interactions. This non-equilibrium spectral transmission model resolves the validity domain of the maximum transmission limit for weakly bonded interfaces and identifies the precise boundary variable governing the crossover under operational conditions, explicitly decoupled from local thermal expansion and equilibrium bulk scattering artifacts.
representatives.core_contribution: The critical interface bonding energy threshold for the bulk-to-interface thermal resistance crossover is not a static material constant, but a flux-dependent parameter defined by the spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations, shifting the validity boundary of the maximum transmission limit under high power density independent of equilibrium thermal expansion.
representatives.central_hypothesis: The critical interface bonding energy threshold for the bulk-to-interface thermal resistance crossover shifts predictably as a function of the spectral overlap of non-equilibrium phonon populations, mediated by anharmonic interactions, under high heat flux, independent of local thermal expansion or equilibrium temperature-dependent bulk scattering.
representatives.mechanism_or_relation: Flux-dependent spectral transmission threshold mediated by anharmonic phonon interactions, decoupled from equilibrium thermal expansion and bulk scattering
representatives.expected_mechanism: High-power-density heat flux generates a non-equilibrium population of hot phonons, which alters the effective transmission probability and spectral overlap at the interface via anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions, thereby shifting the critical bonding energy threshold where interface resistance overtakes bulk resistance, distinct from shifts caused by local thermal expansion or equilibrium Umklapp scattering.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Observation of a predictable shift in the critical interface bonding energy threshold under varying heat flux densities that persists when local thermal expansion is mechanically constrained and when bulk phonon mean free path is decoupled via isotopic mean free path ablation.
representatives.boundary_or_failure_condition: The model fails when high power density heat flux stress induces irreversible interface reconstruction, defect generation, bulk thermal runaway, or when local thermal expansion dominates the interface contact mechanics.
representatives.claim_scope: Valid for phononic interface systems with weakly to moderately bonded interfaces under quasi-steady-state high heat flux, strictly bounded to regimes where local thermal expansion, stress-induced interface reconstruction, and equilibrium bulk Umklapp scattering are decoupled or accounted for, and before irreversible structural reconstruction or bulk thermal runaway occurs.
assumptions: Non-equilibrium hot phonon populations can be maintained quasi-steady-state via high-repetition-rate ultrafast pumping without causing immediate thermal damage or intermixing.
Anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions are the primary driver of the altered spectral overlap under these non-equilibrium conditions.
Local thermal expansion and stress-induced contact area changes are mechanically constrained or quantitatively decoupled from the spectral transmission measurements.
representatives.gap_alignment: Resolves the unmapped boundary variable by defining it as a flux-dependent spectral overlap parameter. Clarifies the boundary condition regarding the predictive applicability of the model for weakly bonded interfaces by explicitly bounding out thermal expansion confounders.
representatives.evidence_requirement: Quantitative mapping of the critical interface bonding energy threshold as a function of heat flux density, corroborated by spectral phonon characterization, isotopic ablation to isolate non-equilibrium phonon effects, and mechanical constraint of the interface to rule out thermal expansion artifacts.
representatives.evidence_basis: Ultrafast spectral phonon characterization of mechanically constrained Si/Ge heterostructures under varying heat flux densities and isotopic compositions.
representatives.falsifier: Demonstration that the threshold shift vanishes when non-equilibrium phonons are present but thermal expansion is unconstrained, or that the shift is entirely explained by bulk temperature-dependent thermal conductivity changes and equilibrium Umklapp scattering without requiring a non-equilibrium spectral overlap model.

representatives.title: Adaptive Spectral Phonon Steering: Closed-Loop Partition of Phonon and Electron Heat Conduction in High-Power-Density Wide-Bandgap Semiconductors
representatives.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum heat dissipation in high-power-density materials remain entangled because open-loop carrier-density sweeps cannot adaptively resolve overlapping transport signatures. We invert the standard premise that characterization is a passive readout: spectral phonon characterization becomes an active steering signal that directly drives the next carrier-density and temperature perturbation, pushing the system toward the partition boundary where phonon and electron contributions become maximally distinguishable. Applied to electrostatically gated β-Ga2O3 and doped GaN thin films on micro-bridge devices, this feedback-closed-loop protocol converges on a self-calibrated phonon-electron partition that open-loop methods cannot resolve. The loop breaks down when strong electron-phonon coupling exceeds the perturbability boundary, or when bipolar thermal transport or contact resistance variations confound the bulk signal, defining the validity domain of the partition.
representatives.core_contribution: Inverting characterization from passive readout to active steering signal: real-time phonon mean-free-path distributions from mode-resolved inelastic scattering and transient thermal grating spectroscopy directly drive carrier-density and temperature perturbations, creating a self-calibrating observation protocol that adaptively converges on the phonon-electron heat-conduction partition boundary under high power density, bounded by the extrinsic regime and invariant contact resistance.
representatives.central_hypothesis: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density wide-bandgap semiconductors can be discriminated by exploiting the differential response of each carrier type to controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, with mode-resolved inelastic scattering serving as an active steering signal that drives the system toward the partition boundary where phonon and electron contributions become maximally distinguishable, provided the system is restricted to the extrinsic regime to eliminate bipolar transport and contact thermal resistance is invariant or independently calibrated.
representatives.mechanism_or_relation: Differential response of phonon and electron heat conduction carriers to controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, exploited via closed-loop feedback where mode-resolved inelastic scattering steers perturbation toward the partition boundary, contingent on the absence of bipolar transport and invariant interfacial thermal resistance.
representatives.expected_mechanism: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling, after decoupling inelastic polar optical phonon scattering effects), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By using mode-resolved inelastic scattering and transient thermal grating spectroscopy to compute a distinguishability metric D(n,T) that quantifies separation between phonon and electron spectral signatures, the feedback loop steers perturbations toward conditions where D is maximized, thereby isolating each carrier's contribution to total thermal conductivity and partitioning the maximum heat dissipation capacity, provided bipolar transport is suppressed and contact resistance is invariant.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Convergence of the phonon-electron partition ratio to within 5% over three consecutive feedback iterations, with the closed-loop protocol achieving >3× higher partition precision (lower uncertainty in phonon vs. electron thermal conductivity decomposition) compared to open-loop grid-based perturbation at equivalent measurement effort, while confirming negligible bipolar contribution and invariant contact resistance.
representatives.boundary_or_failure_condition: The feedback loop breaks down and the partition becomes invalid when strong electron-phonon coupling causes the electron-phonon drag time τ_ep to fall below ~1 ps, when power density exceeds the material's thermal runaway threshold, when the temperature enters the intrinsic regime causing bipolar thermal transport to dominate, or when gate-induced variations in interfacial contact thermal resistance exceed the bulk signal, causing the distinguishability metric D(n,T) to oscillate or diverge.
representatives.claim_scope: Wide-bandgap semiconductors (β-Ga2O3, GaN) and metallic thin films (TiN) under high power density (up to 2 kW/cm^2), moderate electron-phonon coupling regime (τ_ep > 1 ps), temperatures 100–600 K, heavily doped extrinsic carrier densities (10^18–10^20 cm^-3) to suppress bipolar thermal transport, with explicit decoupling of polar optical phonon scattering effects on the Lorenz number and invariant or independently calibrated micro-bridge interfacial thermal resistance.
assumptions: Phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly temperature-dependent via Umklapp scattering; electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via Wiedemann-Franz in moderate-coupling regime after decoupling polar optical phonon scattering; mode-resolved inelastic scattering and transient thermal grating spectroscopy can resolve phonon mean-free-path distributions from electronic excitations with sufficient energy resolution; the system remains in the extrinsic regime to prevent bipolar thermal transport; interfacial contact thermal resistance is invariant under gating or independently calibrated.
representatives.gap_alignment: Resolved by the closed-loop convergence trajectory itself serving as the discriminating observation that partitions carrier contributions, while explicitly bounding bipolar and contact resistance confounders. Resolved by making the differential carrier response an actively exploited control variable, providing mechanistic evidence for phonon-electron partitioning. Resolved by stress-testing the feedback loop under extreme conditions to explicitly identify where strong coupling, bipolar transport, or contact variations invalidate the partition premise.
representatives.evidence_requirement: Direct observation of partition ratio convergence under closed-loop vs. open-loop perturbation protocols, mode-resolved phonon mean-free-path distributions from inelastic scattering showing spectral separation from electronic excitations, confirmation of negligible bipolar thermal conductivity in the extrinsic regime, and identification of the coupling-strength or contact-resistance boundary where feedback divergence occurs.
representatives.evidence_basis: Mode-resolved phonon mean-free-path distributions from inelastic scattering and transient thermal grating spectroscopy, partition ratio convergence metrics under closed-loop vs. open-loop protocols, and identification of coupling-strength and confounder failure boundaries.
representatives.falsifier: Demonstration that phonon and electron contributions cannot be independently varied or measured with sufficient precision to distinguish their relative contributions, that Wiedemann-Franz deviations are dominated by inelastic polar optical phonon scattering rather than electron-phonon coupling, or that bipolar thermal transport or contact resistance variations inherently dominate the total thermal resistance signal under the required gating conditions.
representatives.risks: ['Risk 1: Strong electron-phonon coupling in certain materials causes the Lorenz ratio to deviate >20% from Wiedemann-Franz, making carrier contributions non-perturbable independently. Mitigation: Pre-screen materials via low-temperature electrical/thermal conductivity ratios; restrict feedback protocol to moderate-coupling regime where electron-phonon drag time τ_ep > 1 ps.', 'Risk 2: Inelastic polar optical phonon scattering in wide-bandgap semiconductors inherently breaks the Wiedemann-Franz law, confounding the feedback metric. Mitigation: Explicitly model and decouple polar optical phonon scattering contributions to the Lorenz number before computing the distinguishability metric D(n,T).', 'Risk 3: Spectral phonon characterization lacks energy resolution to separate low-frequency phonons from electronic excitations, causing feedback to chase noise. Mitigation: Use mode-resolved inelastic scattering with <5 meV resolution; implement convergence criteria requiring signal-to-noise ratio >10 before feedback update.', 'Risk 4: High-temperature electrostatic gating (up to 600 K) may fail due to dielectric breakdown or gate leakage. Mitigation: Use crystalline HfO2 gate dielectrics with breakdown field >5 MV/cm; monitor gate leakage current and abort if exceeding 1 μA/cm^2.', 'Risk 5: Bipolar thermal transport at high temperatures or gate-induced contact resistance changes could confound the bulk partition signal. Mitigation: Strictly limit operation to the heavily doped extrinsic regime (n > 10^18 cm^-3) and independently calibrate or verify the invariance of micro-bridge contact thermal resistance.']

representatives.title: Moiré Potential Landscapes Dictate the Thermal Cycling Stability of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
representatives.abstract: Engineered interlayer twist angles suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures, but their stability under operational thermal cycling remains unverified across diverse materials. We replace the complex shear-strain locking mechanism with a fundamental boundary condition governed by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape. We demonstrate that engineered twist angles remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, and in the absence of confounding defect-mediated or chemically-induced pinning. By synthesizing heterostructures across diverse material families and subjecting them to controlled thermal cycling, we isolate the moiré potential mechanism and establish the material-dependent limits of thermal anisotropy retention.
representatives.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy under operational thermal cycling is strictly bounded by a critical interlayer binding energy threshold dictated by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, specifically in regimes where defect-mediated and chemically-induced interlayer pinning are negligible.
representatives.central_hypothesis: Engineered interlayer twist angles designed to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, and in the absence of confounding defect-mediated or chemically-induced interlayer pinning.
representatives.mechanism_or_relation: The twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape creates fundamental energy barriers that pin specific twist angles, dictating the critical threshold for interlayer binding energy and structural stability under thermal stress, distinct from and dominant over defect-mediated or chemical pinning mechanisms.
representatives.expected_mechanism: The twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape creates fundamental energy barriers that pin specific twist angles. When the interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, and defect-mediated or chemical pinning is negligible, the engineered twist angles persist, maintaining suppressed cross-plane thermal conductivity; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Compare the retention of cross-plane thermal anisotropy across different van der Waals material families with varying moiré potential depths but similar intrinsic defect densities, or utilize low-temperature cycling regimes to suppress chemical bonding, thereby isolating the moiré potential mechanism via a material-dependent binding energy ablation.
representatives.boundary_or_failure_condition: The structural stability of the engineered twist angles fails when the interlayer binding energy falls below the critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, or when defect-mediated pinning and interlayer chemical bonding become the dominant retention mechanisms, masking the true moiré potential threshold.
representatives.claim_scope: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in van der Waals heterostructures under operational thermal cycling, bounded by the moiré potential landscape in regimes free from defect-mediated or chemically-induced interlayer pinning.
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy and moiré potential depths can be accurately calculated or measured for diverse van der Waals material families.
Thermal cycling conditions can be selected to minimize interlayer diffusion and chemical bonding, ensuring moiré potential pinning is the dominant retention mechanism.
representatives.gap_alignment: The replacement of the shear-strain locking mechanism with the moiré potential landscape directly addresses the missing assumption of structural stability under operation for engineered twist angles, while the material-dependent ablation protocol and explicit bounding of defect-mediated confounders resolves the material generality boundary condition.
representatives.evidence_requirement: Measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity before and after sustained thermal cycling across diverse van der Waals heterostructures, correlated with their calculated moiré potential energy barriers and interlayer binding energies, to confirm the critical energy threshold for structural stability in the absence of defect or chemical pinning.
representatives.evidence_basis: Measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity before and after sustained thermal cycling across diverse van der Waals heterostructures, correlated with their calculated moiré potential energy barriers.
representatives.falsifier: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking within device-relevant thermal cycling conditions in the absence of defect-mediated or chemical pinning, resulting in recovery of cross-plane conductivity to within 20% of pristine aligned values.
representatives.risks: Primary risk is that thermal cycling could induce interlayer diffusion or chemical bonding (e.g., via chalcogen vacancies) that pins the layers, providing an alternative explanation for the retention of thermal anisotropy independent of moiré potential pinning. Mitigation involves using low-temperature cycling regimes and verifying structural integrity via cross-sectional TEM to rule out chemical bridging. Secondary risk is that thermal contact resistance changes during cycling could mimic changes in intrinsic cross-plane thermal conductivity. Mitigation involves using suspended membrane geometries and time-domain thermoreflectance to decouple contact resistance from intrinsic material properties.

representatives.title: Dynamic Twist-Angle Relaxation and Thermal Transport Limits in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides under High Power Density
representatives.abstract: We invert the static structural assumption of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy by demonstrating that high power density induces dynamic interlayer slip, fundamentally limiting cross-plane heat dissipation. By closing a feedback loop between in-situ thermal metrology and electron diffraction, we map the structural degradation of MoS2/WS2 and other TMDs during thermal cycling. This reveals a shared mechanism where hot-phonon drag (phonon wind) drives moiré superlattice translation and rotation, establishing a critical pinning energy threshold that bounds the maximum thermal transport limit. Our work resolves the unmapped phenomenon of interfacial thermal saturation and provides direct observation of the structural failure boundary, explicitly decoupled from macroscopic delamination and defect-mediated scattering.
representatives.core_contribution: The fundamental limit of cross-plane thermal transport in twisted TMDs under high power density is not a static phonon-scattering ceiling, but a dynamic structural instability where phonon-wind-driven moiré superlattice translation and rotation form a closed-loop failure mechanism bounded by critical interfacial pinning energy, explicitly decoupled from macroscopic delamination and defect generation.
representatives.central_hypothesis: Under high power density, the cross-plane thermal transport limit in twisted TMDs is governed by phonon-wind-driven moiré superlattice translation and rotation exceeding local pinning energies, bounded by a critical interfacial binding energy, while explicitly excluding macroscopic thermomechanical delamination and defect-mediated scattering.
representatives.mechanism_or_relation: Hot-phonon drag (phonon wind) exerts a lateral force on the moiré superlattice that exceeds the local pinning energy, inducing coherent interlayer slip and twist-angle relaxation, thereby increasing interfacial thermal resistance in a positive feedback loop, distinct from macroscopic buckling or point-defect scattering.
representatives.expected_mechanism: Phonon-wind-driven lateral forces exceed the moiré pinning energy, causing coherent interlayer slip that dynamically alters the moiré superlattice, creating a feedback loop that increases interfacial thermal resistance until the critical binding energy threshold is breached, without invoking macroscopic delamination or defect generation.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Direct observation of coherent moiré superlattice translation and twist-angle distribution broadening via in-situ electron diffraction during thermal cycling, contrasted with isothermal mechanical controls and defect-free static twist-angle controls, to isolate the phonon-wind-driven slip component from pure thermomechanical expansion and defect-mediated scattering.
representatives.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds up to the critical pinning energy threshold where coherent interlayer slip becomes irreversible; beyond this, the structural state fails via macroscopic delamination, and thermal transport saturates at the maximum interfacial thermal resistance limit, exiting the scope of the coherent slip mechanism.
representatives.claim_scope: Nanoscale transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures under high power density thermal loading, specifically bounded to regimes where phonon-wind-driven moiré superlattice translation exceeds local pinning energies, excluding macroscopic delamination, blistering, and defect-mediated scattering.
assumptions: The twist-angle distribution and moiré superlattice translation can be accurately quantified via in-situ electron diffraction without beam-induced damage.
MD force fields adequately capture the critical pinning energy for coherent interlayer slip distinct from macroscopic delamination.
Phonon-wind-driven slip can be experimentally decoupled from pure thermomechanical expansion and defect generation using isothermal mechanical controls and defect-free baselines.
representatives.gap_alignment: The in-situ feedback loop directly provides the missing direct_observation of thermal saturation via coherent moiré slip, while the phonon-wind mechanism resolves the unmapped phenomenon of interfacial thermal resistance limits, strictly bounded against confounding delamination and defect effects.
representatives.evidence_requirement: Quantitative measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation correlated with in-situ electron diffraction metrics of coherent moiré superlattice translation and twist-angle distribution changes, validated against MD-derived critical pinning energy thresholds and strictly decoupled from thermomechanical expansion and defect-generation baselines.
representatives.evidence_basis: Cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements correlated with electron diffraction metrics of coherent moiré translation and twist-angle distribution changes, validated against MD-derived critical pinning energy thresholds.
representatives.falsifier: Evidence that twist-angle broadening and thermal degradation occur entirely due to macroscopic thermomechanical delamination, blistering, or defect generation (e.g., chalcogen vacancies) without any coherent phonon-wind-driven interlayer slip, or that the thermal transport limit is strictly governed by static phonon scattering without dynamic moiré superlattice degradation.
representatives.risks: The primary risk is that the in-situ electron diffraction lacks the spatiotemporal resolution to capture transient coherent moiré slip before macroscopic failure, or that defect generation under high power density cannot be fully suppressed or decoupled from the phonon-wind effect in the experimental setup.

representatives.title: Stability Boundaries of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Under High Power Density
representatives.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered moiré interfaces are hypothesized to tune interfacial thermal resistance via coherent phonon scattering, but their structural stability under high power density remains unverified. We invert the premise of static structural stability, positing that high power density thermomechanical stress induces twist-angle relaxation and decohesion, shifting the scattering mechanism and creating a dynamic thermal transport ceiling. By closing the loop between ultrafast thermal characterization and interfacial atomic structure evolution, we quantify twist-angle degradation via nanodiffraction and cross-plane thermal resistance via time-domain thermoreflectance. Molecular dynamics determine critical binding energy thresholds, validated across MoS2/WS2 and extended to MoSe2/WSe2. Crucially, we isolate twist-angle relaxation from confounding defect generation and interfacial blistering to establish the true material-dependent limits of heat transfer in metastable nanoscale heterostructures.
representatives.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is inherently metastable under high power density; the true limit of interfacial thermal transport is governed by a dynamic feedback loop between high-power-density-induced twist-angle relaxation and the resulting shift from coherent moiré to incoherent phonon scattering, distinct from defect-mediated or blistering-induced thermal resistance.
representatives.central_hypothesis: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is inherently metastable under high power density; the true limit of interfacial thermal transport is governed by a dynamic feedback loop between high-power-density-induced twist-angle relaxation and the resulting shift from coherent moiré to incoherent phonon scattering.
representatives.expected_mechanism: High power density thermomechanical stress induces twist-angle relaxation and van der Waals decohesion, which destroys the coherent moiré superlattice, shifting the interfacial phonon scattering mechanism from coherent to incoherent and creating a dynamic thermal transport ceiling.
representatives.discriminating_observation: Cross-plane thermal conductivity measured via time-domain thermoreflectance before and after high power density thermal stress, correlated with twist-angle distribution changes quantified via ultrafast electron diffraction and nanodiffraction, while explicitly ruling out defect generation via Raman mapping and interfacial blistering via cross-sectional STEM.
representatives.boundary_or_failure_condition: Critical binding energy thresholds where twist-angle relaxation saturates, determined via molecular dynamics calibrated against experimental ultrafast thermal characterization.
representatives.claim_scope: Limits of Heat Transfer in Matter, specifically interfacial thermal resistance and phonon scattering mechanisms in nanoscale transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures under high power density thermomechanical stress, contingent on distinguishing twist-angle relaxation from defect generation and blistering.
assumptions: High power density thermomechanical stress induces van der Waals decohesion and twist-angle relaxation in metastable TMD heterostructures.
High power density induces uniform twist-angle relaxation rather than localized defect generation or macroscopic interfacial blistering.
representatives.gap_alignment: Addresses the unmapped phenomenon of thermal saturation and the unmapped target object of nanoscale electronic materials by identifying twist-angle relaxation under high power density as the governing mechanism.
representatives.evidence_requirement: Measurement of cross-plane thermal conductivity and twist-angle distribution via time-domain thermoreflectance and ultrafast electron diffraction before and after high power density thermal stress, contrasted with molecular dynamics predictions of critical binding energy thresholds, alongside structural validation to exclude defects and blistering.
representatives.evidence_basis: Direct observation of thermal transport ceilings and twist-angle degradation in nanoscale transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures under high power density conditions.
representatives.falsifier: Evidence that the selected gaps require mutually incompatible mechanisms, that twist-angle relaxation does not occur under high power density thermomechanical stress, or that the observed thermal ceiling is entirely attributable to defect generation or interfacial blistering rather than twist-angle relaxation.
representatives.risks: Risk 1: Ultrafast electron diffraction may lack the spatial resolution to detect sub-nanometer twist-angle relaxation. Mitigation: Combine with cross-sectional STEM and Raman mapping to corroborate structural changes. Risk 2: Molecular dynamics forcefields may not accurately capture the van der Waals decohesion under thermal stress. Mitigation: Calibrate MD binding energy thresholds directly against the experimental ultrafast thermal characterization data. Risk 3: High power density may cause defect generation or blistering rather than uniform twist-angle relaxation. Mitigation: Use cross-sectional STEM and Raman mapping to verify the absence of point defects and macroscopic delamination, isolating twist-angle relaxation as the primary structural change.

representatives.title: Thermally-Induced Moiré Lattice Relaxation and the Collapse of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
representatives.abstract: Twist-angle engineering in van der Waals heterostructures promises unprecedented control over cross-plane thermal transport, but assumes structural invariance under thermal loading. We invert this premise, demonstrating that twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is structurally metastable and collapses when thermal loading exceeds critical interlayer binding energy thresholds. By combining high heat flux thermal loading with nanobeam electron diffraction and molecular dynamics across MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides, we reveal a thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation mechanism. This establishes the fundamental interfacial thermal resistance limit under high heat flux, shifting the paradigm from continuous intrinsic phonon scattering to dynamic structural stability boundaries in nanoscale heat dissipation.
representatives.core_contribution: The fundamental limit of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport is defined not by continuous intrinsic interfacial phonon scattering or macroscopic delamination, but by the critical interlayer binding energy threshold governing abrupt, thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation under high heat flux.
representatives.central_hypothesis: The fundamental limit of twist-angle-engineered cross-plane thermal transport under high heat flux is not governed by continuous intrinsic anharmonic phonon scattering or macroscopic delamination, but collapses dynamically via an abrupt step-change when thermal loading exceeds the critical interlayer binding energy threshold, triggering sub-nanometer thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation.
