assumptions: Wiedemann-Franz law deviations can be attributed primarily to electron-phonon coupling rather than other scattering mechanisms
Spectral phonon imaging has sufficient resolution to distinguish phonon contributions from electron contributions
Carrier density variations do not significantly alter phonon dispersion or scattering rates
The material system allows independent control of carrier density without introducing additional defect scattering
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

route_signature.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

competitive_ideas.title: Feedback-Stabilized Mode-Resolved Phonon Invariant for Partitioning Heat Conduction in High-Power-Density Materials
competitive_ideas.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials are conventionally partitioned using the macroscopic Wiedemann-Franz law, which fails under strong electron-phonon coupling. We replace this weak macroscopic partitioning with a closed-loop stabilized mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant, restricted to decoupled high-frequency optical phonon modes. By applying controlled carrier density, temperature, and coherent THz phonon pumping perturbations to a doped wide-bandgap semiconductor, we use ultrafast spectral phonon imaging to track the mode-resolved phonon mean free path distribution. A feedback loop adjusts the perturbation trajectory to maintain this phonon population invariant, effectively freezing the targeted optical phonon contribution. To address the confounding risk of perturbation-induced acoustic phonon scattering, the invariant maintenance is strictly bounded to regimes where the dominant heat-carrying acoustic phonon population remains invariant or is independently quantifiable. This enables the direct isolation of the electron thermal conductivity. Ablation against open-loop perturbation and stress testing near the thermal damage threshold confirm the identifiability of the partition and bound the validity domain where macroscopic laws fail.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Replacing macroscopic Wiedemann-Franz partitioning with a feedback-stabilized, mode-resolved non-equilibrium phonon population invariant for decoupled high-frequency optical modes, strictly bounded against perturbation-induced acoustic phonon alterations, enables the direct isolation of electron heat conduction under high-power-density conditions where traditional kinetic models break down.
competitive_ideas.method:
Conceptual move: Replace the assumption of macroscopic thermal equilibrium (Wiedemann-Franz) with a direct, mode-resolved structural invariant (phonon MFP distribution) that is actively maintained via closed-loop feedback while varying electronic states.
1. Synthesize a heavily doped wide-bandgap semiconductor (e.g., n-type 4H-SiC) as the high_power_density_material.
2. Apply carrier_density_temperature_perturbation via electrostatic gating and resistive heating to sweep carrier density across the metal-insulator transition while varying temperature.
3. Perform spectral_phonon_imaging using ultrafast energy-resolved X-ray diffraction to extract the mode-resolved phonon mean free path (MFP) distribution in real-time.
4. Implement the mode_resolved_non_equilibrium_phonon_population_invariant: compute the deviation of the measured mode-resolved MFP distribution from a baseline reference (mode_resolved_phonon_mfp_deviation_signal). When the deviation exceeds a threshold, adjust the gating voltage and temperature ramp (gating_voltage_and_temperature_ramp_adjustment) to restore the phonon MFP invariant.
5. With the phonon contribution structurally frozen by the invariant, measure the total thermal conductivity; the residual change directly yields the electron heat conduction contribution, bypassing the macroscopic_Wiedemann_Franz_partitioning.
6. Execute the open_loop_perturbation_ablation_protocol: repeat the sweep without the invariant-maintenance feedback (fixed step sizes) to demonstrate that the open-loop approach fails to isolate the electron contribution due to concurrent phonon scattering changes.
7. Execute the thermal_damage_boundary_stress_protocol: push the feedback loop to its maximum correction rates under extreme Joule heating to identify the boundary where the invariant cannot be maintained without structural degradation, explicitly defining the validity domain.
competitive_ideas.risks: ['1. Synchrotron beamtime latency and data processing delays may prevent true real-time feedback, degrading the loop to a slow iterative search that could miss transient separable states or induce thermal damage during the search. Mitigation: Use predictive kinematic models to pre-compensate for known latency, restricting the feedback bandwidth to the thermal diffusion timescale.', '2. Isothermal electrostatic gating at high power densities may be impossible due to unavoidable Joule heating, violating the isothermal assumption and confounding the phonon/electron separation. Mitigation: Explicitly map the thermal gradient field using the spectral phonon imaging and incorporate the gradient into the invariant definition, bounding the claim to the identified validity domain.', '3. Ultrafast X-ray diffraction may lack the energy resolution to separate low-frequency phonon modes from electronic excitations in strongly correlated regimes. Mitigation: Restrict the invariant-maintenance feedback to high-frequency optical phonon modes where separation is clear, and use the stress protocol to bound the failure regime.', '4. Coherent THz phonon pumping may introduce non-linear phonon-phonon scattering (e.g., Klemens or Ridley processes) that alters the targeted invariant. Mitigation: Operate the THz pump below the threshold for anharmonic decay and explicitly monitor for secondary phonon generation.', '5. The perturbations used to freeze optical phonons may inadvertently alter the population or mean free path of the dominant heat-carrying acoustic phonons via changes in phonon-phonon (Umklapp) or electron-acoustic phonon scattering. Mitigation: Concurrently monitor the acoustic phonon mean free path distribution; if it changes, restrict the claim scope to regimes where this change is independently quantifiable and subtractable, or abort the isolation if the acoustic perturbation exceeds the quantification threshold.']
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the identifiability_gap by replacing a failing macroscopic proxy with a direct, feedback-stabilized structural observation. It resolves the mechanism_explanation_gap by providing a causal chain from phonon population invariance to isolated electron transport. The ablation and stress protocols explicitly bound the validity domain, resolving the missing_boundary_condition and invalid_generalization defects.

evaluation.fairness_protocol: The open-loop perturbation ablation protocol serves as the primary comparator, demonstrating that without the invariant-maintenance feedback, the electron contribution cannot be isolated due to concurrent phonon scattering changes.
evaluation.feedback: The proposal successfully addresses the identifiability, mechanism, and boundary gaps by introducing a feedback-stabilized phonon invariant. The use of closed-loop control to actively maintain a structural state is a strong bridge_builder application. However, feasibility is heavily constrained by the latency of ultrafast X-ray diffraction and the physical impossibility of perfectly isothermal gating at high power densities. The mitigation strategies are conceptually sound but will require significant experimental refinement to ensure the feedback loop operates within the thermal diffusion timescale.
evaluation.defect_fix_summary: The feedback-closed-loop skill addressed the identifiability_gap and mechanism_explanation_gap by replacing a passive macroscopic proxy with an active, feedback-stabilized structural invariant that causally isolates electron heat conduction. The thermal_damage_boundary_stress_protocol addressed the missing_boundary_condition and invalid_generalization defects by explicitly defining the validity domain where the invariant can be maintained without structural degradation.

competitive_ideas.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum achievable heat dissipation in high-power-density materials remain obscured by aggregate thermal measurements. We introduce a discriminating observation protocol that replaces unpartitioned thermal transport assumptions with controlled variations in carrier density and temperature, exploiting the differential scaling of electron and phonon conductivities. By coupling this perturbation with spectral phonon imaging to directly visualize phonon mean free paths and scattering rates, we isolate the phonon-limited regime from the electron-limited regime. This mechanism-commit innovation resolves the identifiability gap in high-power-density thermal transport, establishing explicit validity boundaries for the Wiedemann-Franz law under extreme carrier injection and defining the fundamental limits of heat dissipation.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The unpartitioned phonon and electron heat conduction mechanism in high-power-density materials can be refined into a discriminated, carrier-specific transport model by applying controlled carrier density and temperature variations alongside spectral phonon imaging, thereby isolating the fundamental limits of maximum heat dissipation.
competitive_ideas.method: 1. Conceptual Move: Replace the aggregate phonon_electron_heat_conduction assumption with a differential perturbation strategy (carrier_density_temperature_variation) to decouple carrier responses. 2. Material Synthesis & Perturbation: Synthesize high_power_density_material systems (e.g., doped wide-bandgap semiconductors or metallic thin films). Apply carrier_density_temperature_variation via electrostatic gating and controlled cryogenic-to-ambient temperature sweeps to perturb the electron and phonon populations independently. 3. Discriminating Observation: Utilize spectral_phonon_imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) as the ablation protocol to directly visualize phonon transport pathways, effectively isolating the phonon mean free path distributions from the total thermal signal. 4. Boundary Calibration: Compare the extracted phonon conductivity against the total thermal conductivity to quantify the electron contribution via Wiedemann-Franz deviations, bounding the maximum_heat_dissipation capacity across phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk is the breakdown of the Wiedemann-Franz law in strongly correlated systems, which may confound electron-phonon coupling signatures. Mitigation relies on using spectral_phonon_imaging as an independent, direct observation of the phonon pathway to cross-validate the electronic contribution without relying solely on electrical conductivity extrapolations. A secondary risk is insufficient energy resolution in spectral imaging to distinguish low-frequency phonons from electronic excitations; this is mitigated by restricting the validity domain to temperature and carrier density regimes where phonon Umklapp scattering strictly dominates.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the identifiability and mechanism explanation gaps by replacing the weak, unpartitioned thermal transport assumption with a refined differential perturbation (carrier_density_temperature_variation). The addition of spectral_phonon_imaging as an ablation protocol provides the necessary discriminating observation to back-infer the specific carrier mechanisms, while explicitly bounding the validity domain to prevent invalid generalization under extreme non-equilibrium conditions.

failure_modes: Electrostatic gating may only modulate a thin surface layer (Debye length), failing to perturb the bulk carrier density required to observe a macroscopic change in thermal conductivity in thick high-power-density materials.

evaluation.fairness_protocol: The comparator is the total thermal conductivity measured via standard steady-state or time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) methods, contrasted against the phonon-specific conductivity extracted from spectral phonon imaging. The electron contribution is then isolated by subtraction and compared against the Wiedemann-Franz prediction based on independent electrical conductivity measurements, ensuring a fair decomposition of the transport pathways.
evaluation.feedback: The proposal effectively addresses the identifiability and mechanism gaps by introducing a dual-pronged approach: carrier density variation to perturb the electron population and spectral phonon imaging to directly observe phonon transport. However, the feasibility of electrostatic gating to modulate bulk carrier density in thick high-power-density materials is a significant risk, as gating typically only affects a thin surface layer. Consider using chemical doping or ionic liquid gating to achieve bulk carrier density variation, or explicitly restrict the validity domain to ultra-thin films where gating penetrates the entire volume. Additionally, ensure the spectral phonon imaging protocol explicitly accounts for the energy resolution limits of current XRD setups to avoid underestimating low-frequency phonon contributions.

competitive_ideas.title: Direct Observation of Saturating Interfacial Thermal Conductance in Annealed Graphene/SiO2 Heterostructures Reveals Bonding-Dependent Phonon Transmission Limits
competitive_ideas.abstract: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance fundamentally limits heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing thermal conductance saturation remain unobserved. We demonstrate that interfacial thermal conductance in graphene/SiO2 heterostructures saturates at a critical covalent bond density, revealing a fundamental limit to phonon transmission enhancement through interface engineering. Using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy, we directly observe non-monotonic thermal conductance evolution during controlled annealing, where initial van der Waals-to-covalent bonding transitions increase conductance, but excessive covalent bonding introduces defect scattering that degrades heat transfer. This discriminating observation falsifies monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a bonding-configuration-dependent upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Interfacial thermal conductance exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on covalent bond density, saturating and then degrading due to competing phonon transmission enhancement and defect scattering mechanisms, establishing a fundamental material-dependent limit on thermal transport across engineered interfaces.
competitive_ideas.method: We synthesize graphene/SiO2 van der Waals heterostructures via chemical vapor deposition and dry transfer to create atomically sharp interfaces. We apply controlled thermal annealing (200-600°C in vacuum) to systematically tune interfacial bonding from pure van der Waals to mixed van der Waals-covalent to defect-rich covalent configurations. We characterize the atomic bonding configuration using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy to quantify covalent bond density (C-O-Si bridge bonds) and defect concentration. We measure interfacial thermal conductance using ultrafast thermoreflectance spectroscopy with <10 ps temporal resolution across the annealing series. We ablate the mechanism by comparing as-grown van der Waals interfaces, optimally annealed interfaces at peak conductance, and over-annealed defect-rich interfaces to isolate bonding configuration effects from bulk property changes, directly observing the saturation and degradation of thermal conductance.
competitive_ideas.risks: Risk 1: Annealing may cause graphene degradation rather than controlled interface modification. Mitigation: Use Raman spectroscopy to monitor graphene quality (2D/G ratio) and limit annealing temperature to <600°C where graphene remains intact. Risk 2: Thermal conductance changes may be dominated by bulk SiO2 property changes rather than interface effects. Mitigation: Use thickness-controlled SiO2 samples (>100 nm) and compare with bulk SiO2 thermal conductivity measurements to isolate interface contribution. Risk 3: Ultrafast thermoreflectance may not achieve sufficient sensitivity for sub-nm interface layers. Mitigation: Use high-repetition-rate laser system (80 MHz) and lock-in detection with signal averaging to achieve <1% measurement uncertainty on thermal decay time constants.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the direct_observation gap by providing direct experimental observation of thermal conductance saturation at atomic-scale interfaces under controlled bonding configurations. The verification reversal route ensures the mechanism is back-inferred from observable thermal transport limits rather than assumed a priori. The non-monotonic conductance dependence serves as a pre-registered discriminating outcome that falsifies simple monotonic bonding-conductance models and establishes a fundamental upper bound on interfacial thermal transport.

mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Phonon and electron heat conduction respond differently to changes in carrier density and temperature: electron thermal conductivity scales with electrical conductivity via the Wiedemann-Franz law (with deviations indicating strong electron-phonon coupling), while phonon thermal conductivity is largely insensitive to carrier density but strongly dependent on temperature through Umklapp scattering rates. By systematically varying carrier density (via gating or doping) and measuring thermal conductivity, the electron contribution can be isolated. Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

competitive_ideas.title: Adaptive Spectral Phonon Steering: Closed-Loop Partition of Phonon and Electron Heat Conduction in High-Power-Density Wide-Bandgap Semiconductors
competitive_ideas.abstract: The relative contributions of phonon and electron heat conduction to maximum heat dissipation in high-power-density materials remain entangled because open-loop carrier-density sweeps cannot adaptively resolve overlapping transport signatures. We invert the standard premise that characterization is a passive readout: spectral phonon characterization becomes an active steering signal that directly drives the next carrier-density and temperature perturbation, pushing the system toward the partition boundary where phonon and electron contributions become maximally distinguishable. Applied to electrostatically gated β-Ga2O3 and doped GaN thin films on micro-bridge devices, this feedback-closed-loop protocol converges on a self-calibrated phonon-electron partition that open-loop methods cannot resolve. The loop breaks down when strong electron-phonon coupling exceeds the perturbability boundary, or when bipolar thermal transport or contact resistance variations confound the bulk signal, defining the validity domain of the partition.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Inverting characterization from passive readout to active steering signal: real-time phonon mean-free-path distributions from mode-resolved inelastic scattering and transient thermal grating spectroscopy directly drive carrier-density and temperature perturbations, creating a self-calibrating observation protocol that adaptively converges on the phonon-electron heat-conduction partition boundary under high power density, bounded by the extrinsic regime and invariant contact resistance.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to rewire spectral phonon imaging from a post-hoc diagnostic into an active control variable that steers carrier-density and temperature perturbations toward the phonon-electron partition boundary. (1) Synthesize high-power-density material systems—Si-doped β-Ga2O3 (100) and Mg-doped GaN thin films (50–200 nm)—on suspended SiNx micro-bridge devices with integrated top-gate dielectrics (HfO2, 20 nm) for electrostatic carrier-density control. (2) Apply initial carrier_density_temperature_variation via gated bias (carrier densities 10^17–10^20 cm^-3) and resistive Joule heating across a designed matrix of temperatures (100–600 K) at power densities up to 2 kW/cm^2. (3) Perform spectral_phonon_imaging using ultrafast X-ray diffraction (UXRD) at a synchrotron beamline with <5 meV energy resolution and ~100 fs temporal resolution to extract mode-resolved phonon mean-free-path distributions and scattering rates for acoustic and optical branches. (4) Compute a distinguishability metric D(n,T) quantifying the spectral separation between phonon and electron scattering signatures in the dynamic structure factor S(q,ω). (5) Feed D(n,T) back to update the next carrier_density_temperature_variation perturbation using a bounded gradient-ascent rule: Δn ∝ ∂D/∂n with step-size capped at 10% of the current carrier density to prevent oscillation. (6) Iterate until the phonon-electron partition converges (partition ratio stabilizes within 5% over three consecutive iterations). (7) Ablate the feedback by running identical perturbation matrices in open-loop mode (predefined grid) and compare partition precision and convergence speed. (8) Stress-test at extreme power densities (>2 kW/cm^2) and in strong-coupling regimes (e.g., heavily doped TiN references) to identify failure boundaries where feedback oscillates or diverges due to electron-phonon drag exceeding the perturbability limit.
competitive_ideas.risks: ['Risk 1: Strong electron-phonon coupling in certain materials causes the Lorenz ratio to deviate >20% from Wiedemann-Franz, making carrier contributions non-perturbable independently. Mitigation: Pre-screen materials via low-temperature electrical/thermal conductivity ratios; restrict feedback protocol to moderate-coupling regime where electron-phonon drag time τ_ep > 1 ps.', 'Risk 2: Inelastic polar optical phonon scattering in wide-bandgap semiconductors inherently breaks the Wiedemann-Franz law, confounding the feedback metric. Mitigation: Explicitly model and decouple polar optical phonon scattering contributions to the Lorenz number before computing the distinguishability metric D(n,T).', 'Risk 3: Spectral phonon characterization lacks energy resolution to separate low-frequency phonons from electronic excitations, causing feedback to chase noise. Mitigation: Use mode-resolved inelastic scattering with <5 meV resolution; implement convergence criteria requiring signal-to-noise ratio >10 before feedback update.', 'Risk 4: High-temperature electrostatic gating (up to 600 K) may fail due to dielectric breakdown or gate leakage. Mitigation: Use crystalline HfO2 gate dielectrics with breakdown field >5 MV/cm; monitor gate leakage current and abort if exceeding 1 μA/cm^2.', 'Risk 5: Bipolar thermal transport at high temperatures or gate-induced contact resistance changes could confound the bulk partition signal. Mitigation: Strictly limit operation to the heavily doped extrinsic regime (n > 10^18 cm^-3) and independently calibrate or verify the invariance of micro-bridge contact thermal resistance.']
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the identifiability_gap by providing a concrete discriminating_observation protocol—the closed-loop convergence trajectory itself serves as the observation that partitions carrier contributions. It addresses the mechanism_explanation_gap by making the differential carrier response an actively exploited control variable rather than a passively measured quantity. The stress-test protocol explicitly defines the validity_domain boundary, resolving the missing_boundary_condition defect by identifying where strong electron-phonon coupling invalidates the partition premise.

failure_modes: UXRD may lack the energy and temporal resolution to distinguish low-frequency phonons from electronic excitations in real-time, causing the feedback loop to chase noise or converge on a false partition boundary.
High-temperature electrostatic gating (up to 600 K) may suffer from dielectric breakdown or gate leakage, preventing the necessary carrier density variations to steer the system.

Strong electron-phonon coupling in the targeted regime may cause the Lorenz ratio to deviate significantly, making the carrier contributions non-perturbable independently and causing the feedback loop to diverge.
evaluation.fairness_protocol: The proposal includes an open-loop ablation (predefined grid) to compare partition precision and convergence speed against the closed-loop feedback, providing a fair comparator for the core mechanism. It also uses heavily doped TiN references as a strong-coupling stress test.
evaluation.feedback: The proposal introduces a highly novel mechanism by inverting characterization into an active control variable. However, relying on ultrafast X-ray diffraction (UXRD) to extract both phonon and electron scattering signatures in real-time for a feedback loop risks a measurement_construct_mismatch, as UXRD is primarily sensitive to lattice dynamics and may not adequately resolve electronic excitations at the required temporal resolution. Additionally, the requirement for real-time synchrotron UXRD coupled with high-temperature electrostatic gating introduces significant insufficient_reproducibility concerns, as this bespoke setup may not be accessible or reproducible across independent labs. Consider whether a more accessible pump-probe optical or thermoreflectance technique could serve as the real-time feedback signal, or if the feedback loop can be decoupled from the primary characterization to improve reproducibility.
evaluation.defect_fix_summary: The feedback-closed-loop skill addresses the identifiability_gap by transforming passive spectral phonon imaging into an active steering signal, creating a discriminating observation protocol that adaptively converges on the partition boundary. It also addresses the missing_boundary_condition defect by explicitly stress-testing the loop under extreme power density and strong-coupling conditions to record failure boundaries where electron-phonon coupling invalidates the partition premise.

Simultaneously, spectral phonon imaging (e.g., ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy resolution) can directly visualize phonon mean free path distributions and scattering rates, providing independent validation of the phonon contribution. The maximum heat dissipation capacity is then partitioned into phonon-limited and electron-limited regimes.

competitive_ideas.title: Closed-Loop Spectral Phonon Imaging Reveals Momentum-Resolved Electron-Phonon Bottlenecks in High-Power-Density Heat Dissipation
competitive_ideas.abstract: The maximum heat dissipation capacity of high-power-density materials is limited by momentum-resolved electron-phonon energy exchange bottlenecks invisible to bulk effective-medium characterization. We introduce an iterative quasi-static representation shift: spectral phonon imaging feedback systematically steers carrier density and temperature perturbations across measurement cycles, converging on momentum-space channels where electron-phonon energy exchange stalls, provided intrinsic scattering dominates over extrinsic limits. This protocol partitions phonon and electron thermal conductivity contributions by exploiting their differential perturbation response—phonons are temperature-sensitive but carrier-density-insensitive, while electrons follow the Wiedemann-Franz law. The invariant exposed is energy flux conservation within converged momentum-space channels; divergence signals the validity boundary where strong correlations or dominant extrinsic scattering break the differential response. We validate through open-loop ablation and extreme-condition stress testing, resolving the identifiability gap in phonon-electron partitioning and establishing bounded validity for high-power-density thermal transport models.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Rewiring spectral phonon imaging from a static characterization tool into an iterative quasi-static feedback signal that systematically steers carrier density and temperature perturbation conditions exposes the momentum-resolved electron-phonon energy exchange bottleneck as a convergent invariant in state space, replacing open-loop bulk scattering models with a bounded discriminating observation protocol that explicitly accounts for intrinsic versus extrinsic scattering limits.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to replace open-loop perturbation-measurement characterization with a closed-loop adaptive protocol in which spectral phonon imaging provides real-time feedback that steers carrier density and temperature perturbation conditions toward momentum-space convergence. (1) Synthesize high-power-density materials (doped wide-bandgap semiconductors, metallic thin films) and perturb them under high power density conditions. (2) Characterize phonon transport pathways using spectral phonon imaging (ultrafast X-ray diffraction with energy-momentum resolution) to obtain the non-equilibrium phonon distribution. (3) Rewire spectral phonon imaging feedback to adaptively update carrier density (via electrostatic gating or chemical doping) and temperature gradient conditions, steering the system toward momentum-space channels where the phonon mean-free-path distribution stabilizes. (4) Compare the converged phonon contribution against the electron contribution derived from Wiedemann-Franz deviations to partition maximum heat dissipation. (5) Calibrate momentum-space boundaries using ab initio calculations. (6) Ablate the feedback loop by running open-loop characterization at fixed perturbation points to confirm that only the closed-loop protocol achieves identifiability. (7) Stress test under extreme power density and strong-correlation conditions to map failure boundaries.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk: Sample degradation or thermal drift during iterative perturbation cycles, causing apparent divergence or false convergence. Mitigation: Implement strict thermal equilibration windows and cross-validate baseline states between cycles. Secondary risk: Dominant extrinsic boundary or defect scattering masks the intrinsic electron-phonon bottleneck, leading to false convergence. Mitigation: Restrict validity domain to materials and length scales where intrinsic scattering rates exceed extrinsic rates, verified via baseline mean-free-path characterization. Tertiary risk: Strong non-linear electron-phonon coupling at extreme conditions entangles thermal signatures. Mitigation: Restrict validity domain to materials where the Wiedemann-Franz law holds at baseline.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the identifiability gap by replacing open-loop characterization with a closed-loop adaptive protocol that converges only when phonon and electron contributions are maximally decoupled in momentum space. It addresses the mechanism explanation gap by exposing energy flux conservation as the invariant that distinguishes the momentum-resolved bottleneck from bulk scattering models. The stress protocol establishes the validity boundary, resolving the missing boundary condition defect by defining where strong correlations or non-linear coupling break the differential response invariant.

mature_idea.scientific_object: Twisted multilayer van der Waals heterostructures (MoS2, WS2, WSe2, MoSe2) with controlled interlayer rotation angles
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy in van der Waals materials is sufficient to maintain twist angles under typical device operating temperatures (<400 K)
Moiré potential landscape creates local energy minima that kinetically trap non-equilibrium twist configurations
Thermal cycling does not induce interlayer slip or delamination that would reset the twist angle distribution
The anisotropy ratio (in-plane vs. cross-plane conductivity) is a monotonic function of twist angle disorder
mature_idea.mechanism_or_relation: Interlayer rotational disorder disrupts coherent phonon tunneling across planes, forcing heat to dissipate through incoherent hopping mechanisms that suppress cross-plane conductance. The stability of these rotational configurations under thermal stress is governed by the competition between the moiré potential energy landscape (which pins specific twist angles) and thermal activation energy (which drives relaxation toward equilibrium stacking). When interlayer binding energy exceeds the thermal activation barrier at operational temperatures, the engineered anisotropy persists; otherwise, rotational relaxation degrades the thermal bottleneck.

competitive_ideas.title: Active Strain-Feedback Loop for Topological Defect Pinning of Random Interlayer Rotations in Van Der Waals Heterostructures Under Thermal Cycling
competitive_ideas.abstract: The extreme thermal anisotropy engineered via random interlayer rotations in van der Waals heterostructures conventionally relies on pristine moiré potential landscapes, limiting applicability to high-binding-energy materials. We invert this premise by demonstrating that structural persistence under high-power thermal cycling is governed by topological defect pinning at strain-induced interlayer domain walls, actively maintained via a dynamically modulated strain-feedback mechanism calibrated by in-situ Raman tracking. By synthesizing heterostructures with controlled interlayer dislocation densities on piezoelectric substrates, we lock random rotational configurations against thermal relaxation. This defect-mediated pinning mechanism, dynamically sustained by piezoelectric strain actuation and quasi-static Raman calibration, decouples operational stability from intrinsic interlayer binding energy. Crucially, we discriminate this topological pinning from confounding kinetic trapping by intrinsic point defects or substrate clamping through controlled defect ablation and unactuated substrate comparisons, establishing a robust design paradigm for high-power-density thermal management across diverse van der Waals material systems.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Structural persistence of random interlayer rotations under macroscopic thermal cycling is governed by topological defect pinning at strain-induced domain walls, dynamically sustained via a modulated strain-feedback loop calibrated by Raman spectroscopy, generalizing extreme thermal anisotropy to low-binding-energy van der Waals materials while explicitly discriminating against kinetic trapping by intrinsic point defects or substrate clamping.
competitive_ideas.method: Conceptual move: Replace the assumption of pristine moiré potential pinning with active strain-feedback-driven topological defect pinning to decouple thermal stability from intrinsic interlayer binding energy. Concrete steps: 1. Synthesize van der Waals heterostructures (including low-binding-energy systems like black phosphorus/InSe and standard TMDs) with random interlayer rotations on piezoelectric substrates. 2. Implement the REWIRE(in_situ_raman_moire_tracking -> piezoelectric_strain_actuation) protocol: use in_situ_raman_moire_tracking to monitor the emergence of moiré phonon mode shifts indicating rotational relaxation, which triggers piezoelectric_strain_actuation to dynamically induce strain domain walls and interlayer dislocations that pin the rotational configurations. 3. Characterize the initial cross-plane thermal conductivity using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) to establish the baseline thermal anisotropy. 4. Perform ADD_PROTOCOL(thermal_annealing_defect_ablation): anneal a subset of samples to eliminate the strain domain walls and interlayer defects, then re-characterize the cross-plane thermal conductivity and twist-angle distribution using Raman mapping and cross-sectional TEM to isolate the contribution of the defect pinning mechanism. 5. competitive_ideas.title: Stability-Bounded Dynamic Moiré Potential Modulation for Adaptive Cross-Plane Thermal Conductivity
competitive_ideas.abstract: Dynamic modulation of the moiré potential via mechanical strain offers a pathway to actively tune interfacial thermal conductance and effective cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted van der Waals heterostructures. However, measurement constructs often conflate true moiré-mediated thermal transport changes with structural degradation, such as twist-angle relaxation, or with intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts in the individual layers. We introduce a stability-bounded strain perturbation protocol that restricts dynamic moiré modulation to regimes where the strain energy remains below the interlayer binding energy barrier, preventing twist-angle relaxation. By correlating in situ electron diffraction with cross-plane thermal conductivity during thermal cycling, and comparing against untwisted control heterostructures, we isolate the pure moiré potential contribution from intrinsic bulk phonon shifts. This approach validates the structural stability assumption and extends the adaptive thermal management paradigm from MoS2/WS2 to broader transition metal dichalcogenides.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The establishment of a critical-strain-bounded structural stability condition for strain-mediated moiré potential modulation, ensuring that measured variations in interfacial thermal conductance and effective cross-plane thermal conductivity strictly reflect dynamic moiré landscape alterations rather than irreversible twist-angle relaxation or intrinsic bulk phonon dispersion shifts.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to replace unconstrained strain application with a stability-bounded strain perturbation that enforces critical binding energy thresholds. Concretely, we synthesize twisted MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures. We apply controlled biaxial strain using piezoelectric actuators while simultaneously performing thermal cycling. We characterize the twist-angle distribution via ultrafast electron diffraction before and after cycling to quantify relaxation. We measure cross-plane thermal conductivity using time-domain thermoreflectance. We determine critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics and compare them with experimental relaxation onset. We use the twist-angle relaxation comparator to ablate the structural degradation effect, isolating the pure moiré potential modulation on thermal conductivity.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk is that the critical strain threshold is too low for any measurable thermal modulation, or that intrinsic bulk phonon shifts are too large to be effectively subtracted via controls. Mitigation involves using molecular dynamics to pre-screen transition metal dichalcogenide combinations with higher interlayer binding energies and employing ultra-thin layers to ensure interface-dominated transport.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch defect by explicitly bounding the strain perturbation to a structurally stable regime, ensuring the measured thermal conductivity changes are causally linked to the moiré potential rather than structural degradation. It sharpens the parent idea by transforming a static assumption of twist-angle preservation into a quantifiable, material-dependent boundary condition.

competitive_ideas.title: Bounding Adaptive Cross-Plane Thermal Conductivity in Twisted TMDs via Strain-Mediated Interlayer Registry Modulation
competitive_ideas.abstract: Dynamic modulation of cross-plane thermal conductivity in twisted van der Waals heterostructures is often assumed to arise purely from affine moiré potential changes under strain. We replace this assumption with a refined mechanism of strain-induced local moiré superlattice reconstruction and interlayer registry modulation, where cross-plane thermal transport is governed by the formation and motion of strain solitons. Crucially, we explicitly decouple this mechanism from confounding out-of-plane van der Waals gap expansion (Poisson effect) and intralayer phonon dispersion shifts. By quantifying local registry changes via ultrafast electron diffraction and independently bounding out-of-plane lattice spacing, we establish the structural stability boundary conditions for adaptive thermal management. This approach resolves measurement construct mismatches by isolating pure potential modulation and local structural reconstruction from uniform gap dilation, enabling robust, real-time thermal tuning across diverse transition metal dichalcogenides.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Replacing the assumption of pure affine moiré potential modulation with strain-induced local moiré superlattice reconstruction (e.g., strain solitons) to explicitly bound the structural stability and interlayer binding energy thresholds required for stable adaptive cross-plane thermal conductivity, while rigorously decoupling these effects from out-of-plane van der Waals gap expansion and intralayer phonon shifts.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to replace the weak assumption of affine moiré potential modulation with strain-mediated twist-angle relaxation and interlayer registry modulation. We synthesize twisted MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures. We apply controlled biaxial strain using piezoelectric actuators while measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity via time-domain thermoreflectance. To isolate the refined mechanism, we perform thermal cycling and use ultrafast electron diffraction to quantify twist-angle distribution changes, distinguishing pure potential modulation from structural relaxation. Molecular dynamics simulations determine critical binding energy thresholds for interlayer slip, validated against experimental slip onset. We ablate the structural stability assumption by comparing thermal conductivity before and after thermal cycling, confirming that adaptive tuning is bounded by interlayer registry and binding energy limits.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk is that interlayer slip or structural degradation during thermal cycling irreversibly alters the moiré pattern, falsifying the assumption of reversible adaptive tuning. Mitigation involves establishing strict binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics and restricting operational strain to the elastic regime. A secondary risk is that out-of-plane gap expansion (Poisson effect) dominates the thermal conductivity changes, masking the moiré reconstruction mechanism. Mitigation involves independent measurement of the van der Waals gap thickness and restricting analysis to strain regimes where registry changes outpace uniform gap dilation.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch and missing_boundary_condition defects in the parent idea by replacing the weak assumption of pure moiré potential modulation with a refined mechanism that accounts for twist-angle relaxation and interlayer registry. It sharpens the thesis by explicitly defining the structural stability boundary conditions required for real-time adaptive thermal management, ensuring the causal link between strain and thermal conductivity is physically bounded and experimentally verifiable.

competitive_ideas.title: Direct Observation of Thermal Transport Limits via Thermally-Driven Twist-Angle Relaxation in Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Multilayers
competitive_ideas.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat transfer in twisted van der Waals multilayers are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the structural stability of twist-angle-engineered interfaces under high power density remains unobserved. We replace the assumption of a static interfacial phonon scattering landscape with a refined mechanism of thermally-activated twist-angle relaxation, which structurally reconstructs the moiré superlattice and modulates thermal transport. By applying time-domain thermoreflectance measurements before and after high-power thermal cycling, we directly observe the thermal saturation phenomenon and isolate the structural scattering mechanism, explicitly ruling out confounders such as hot-phonon bottlenecking and irreversible defect generation. Ablation across varying transition metal dichalcogenide multilayers validates the structural stability boundary condition and material generality, quantifying coherent twist-angle distribution changes via electron diffraction and critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Replacing the assumption of a static interfacial phonon scattering landscape with a thermally-activated twist-angle relaxation mechanism to directly observe and bound interfacial thermal resistance limits under high power density, while explicitly excluding defect-mediated and hot-phonon confounders.
competitive_ideas.method: We realize the conceptual move of substituting static scattering models with a dynamic thermally-driven twist-angle relaxation mechanism. We synthesize twisted transition metal dichalcogenide multilayers (e.g., MoS2/WS2 and extending to MoSe2/WSe2) and apply a controlled thermal cycling protocol to perturb the interface. We then employ time-domain thermoreflectance characterization to directly measure the cross-plane interfacial thermal resistance before and after high-power thermal cycling. To ablate the mechanism-commit-innovation delta, we compare thermally-cycled interfaces against static controls, quantifying twist-angle distribution changes via electron diffraction and determining critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics. This isolates the thermally-driven relaxation contribution and validates the structural stability boundary.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk is that thermal cycling induces irreversible interfacial delamination or chemical interdiffusion rather than reversible twist-angle relaxation, confounding the attribution of thermal resistance changes. Mitigation involves bounding the thermal flux and using molecular dynamics to predict critical binding energy thresholds. Negative-transfer risk: Time-domain thermoreflectance models may struggle to decouple the specific twisted interface thermal resistance from bulk TMD thermal conductivity changes or hot-phonon effects; mitigated by cross-validating thermoreflectance signals with electron diffraction structural metrics and explicit hot-phonon modeling.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped phenomenon and evidence role deficit by providing a direct, thermally-cycled observational framework for thermal saturation under high power density. It sharpens the parent idea by validating the structural stability boundary condition and material generality, replacing the weak static scattering assumption with a refined, dynamic twist-angle relaxation mechanism.

competitive_ideas.title: Stability Boundaries of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Under High Power Density
competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered moiré interfaces are hypothesized to tune interfacial thermal resistance via coherent phonon scattering, but their structural stability under high power density remains unverified. We invert the premise of static structural stability, positing that high power density thermomechanical stress induces twist-angle relaxation and decohesion, shifting the scattering mechanism and creating a dynamic thermal transport ceiling. By closing the loop between ultrafast thermal characterization and interfacial atomic structure evolution, we quantify twist-angle degradation via nanodiffraction and cross-plane thermal resistance via time-domain thermoreflectance. Molecular dynamics determine critical binding energy thresholds, validated across MoS2/WS2 and extended to MoSe2/WSe2. Crucially, we isolate twist-angle relaxation from confounding defect generation and interfacial blistering to establish the true material-dependent limits of heat transfer in metastable nanoscale heterostructures.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is inherently metastable under high power density; the true limit of interfacial thermal transport is governed by a dynamic feedback loop between high-power-density-induced twist-angle relaxation and the resulting shift from coherent moiré to incoherent phonon scattering, distinct from defect-mediated or blistering-induced thermal resistance.
competitive_ideas.method: We realize the conceptual move of replacing static structural assumptions with a dynamic stability boundary. First, we synthesize twisted transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures (MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2) with controlled twist angles and apply high power density thermal cycling. Using ultrafast thermal characterization (time-domain thermoreflectance and ultrafast electron diffraction), we measure cross-plane thermal conductivity and quantify twist angle distribution changes before and after cycling. This characterization feedback is used to update the interfacial atomic structure model, specifically determining critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics. We perform a binding_energy_threshold_ablation by comparing MD predictions with and without the feedback-adjusted structural degradation to isolate the contribution of twist-angle relaxation. Finally, we apply high power density thermal stress to identify the failure boundaries where twist-angle relaxation saturates the thermal transport limit.
competitive_ideas.risks: Risk 1: Ultrafast electron diffraction may lack the spatial resolution to detect sub-nanometer twist-angle relaxation. Mitigation: Combine with cross-sectional STEM and Raman mapping to corroborate structural changes. Risk 2: Molecular dynamics forcefields may not accurately capture the van der Waals decohesion under thermal stress. Mitigation: Calibrate MD binding energy thresholds directly against the experimental ultrafast thermal characterization data. Risk 3: High power density may cause defect generation or blistering rather than uniform twist-angle relaxation. Mitigation: Use cross-sectional STEM and Raman mapping to verify the absence of point defects and macroscopic delamination, isolating twist-angle relaxation as the primary structural change.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped phenomenon of thermal saturation by identifying twist-angle relaxation as the hidden variable governing the thermal transport ceiling. It sharpens the parent idea by replacing the assumption of static moiré stability with a dynamic stability boundary, directly addressing the limits of heat transfer in nanoscale heterostructures without shifting to unrelated interface bonding or measurement isolation problems.

competitive_ideas.title: Cyclic Hysteresis and Residual State Mapping of Structural Stability Boundaries in Twist-Angle-Engineered Transition Metal Dichalcogenides Under High Power Density
competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) assumes structural stability under operational thermal loads, but the fundamental limits of this stability under high power density remain unclear. We investigate the thermally induced interfacial strain mechanism to identify the critical strain thresholds governing moiré lattice distortion. By applying incremental high-power-density thermal cycling and quantifying residual changes in cross-plane thermal conductivity and moiré diffraction spot splitting via time-domain thermoreflectance and nanobeam electron diffraction, we isolate the onset of irreversible interfacial strain accumulation from reversible phonon-phonon scattering. This approach maps the structural stability boundaries across MoS2/WS2 and other TMDs, establishing precise power-density limits where moiré phonon localization degrades due to permanent strain-induced moiré distortion, while strictly bounding the system below the threshold for interfacial decohesion.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is bounded by a critical interfacial strain threshold for moiré lattice distortion, which can be precisely mapped by tracking residual hysteresis in cross-plane Kapitza resistance and moiré diffraction spot splitting across incremental thermal cycling, isolating the irreversible thermally induced interfacial strain mechanism from transient phonon scattering and avoiding high-risk decohesion regimes.
competitive_ideas.method: We realize the cyclic hysteresis mechanism by wiring residual_kapitza_resistance_and_moire_diffraction_hysteresis to incremental_thermal_cycling_bound_adjustment. First, we synthesize twist-angle-engineered MoS2/WS2 and other TMD heterostructures. We apply incremental_pulsed_laser_thermal_cycling via incremental pulsed-laser thermal cycling. After each cycle, we measure the residual cross-plane thermal conductivity via TDTR and quantify residual twist-angle distribution changes via NBED to map the hysteresis loop. The incremental_thermal_cycling_bound_adjustment updates the thermal cycling bounds based on this residual state to pinpoint the onset of irreversible structural degradation. To isolate the contribution of the hysteresis mapping, we perform an open_loop_thermal_cycling_ablation, applying fixed thermal loads without residual tracking. Finally, we conduct an extreme_power_density_stress_test to push the system beyond the predicted critical binding energy threshold, validating the failure boundary against molecular dynamics simulations of interfacial decohesion.
competitive_ideas.risks: The primary risk is that thermal cycling may induce irreversible phase transitions or point defect generation rather than pure interfacial strain, confounding the strain threshold. Mitigation involves correlating the residual thermal conductivity drop with specific NBED and Raman signatures to decouple phase changes and point defects from interfacial strain. Another risk is that residual measurements might miss transient effects, which is mitigated by focusing the analysis strictly on the irreversible strain regime bounded by molecular dynamics predictions.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped phenomenon and target object gaps by providing direct, empirical evidence of thermal transport limits in nanoscale TMD devices under high power density. By replacing the latency-prone real-time feedback loop with a cyclic hysteresis and residual state mapping mechanism, we eliminate control-system artifacts and thermal lag, proving that twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is fundamentally limited by thermally activated interfacial decohesion.

competitive_ideas.title: Thermally-Induced Moiré Lattice Relaxation and the Collapse of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle engineering in van der Waals heterostructures promises unprecedented control over cross-plane thermal transport, but assumes structural invariance under thermal loading. We invert this premise, demonstrating that twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is structurally metastable and collapses when thermal loading exceeds critical interlayer binding energy thresholds. By combining high heat flux thermal loading with nanobeam electron diffraction and molecular dynamics across MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides, we reveal a thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation mechanism. This establishes the fundamental interfacial thermal resistance limit under high heat flux, shifting the paradigm from continuous intrinsic phonon scattering to dynamic structural stability boundaries in nanoscale heat dissipation.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The fundamental limit of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport is defined not by continuous intrinsic interfacial phonon scattering or macroscopic delamination, but by the critical interlayer binding energy threshold governing abrupt, thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation under high heat flux.
competitive_ideas.method: We invert the static twist-angle premise by subjecting the nanoscale semiconductor interface (MoS2/WS2 and compositionally varied TMDs via interface composition control) to high-power-density thermal cycling in ultra-high vacuum. We measure the interfacial thermal resistance limit before and after cycling to quantify degradation. We use nanobeam electron diffraction to directly observe twist angle distribution changes, linking macroscopic thermal degradation to the thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation mechanism. Molecular dynamics simulations determine the critical binding energy thresholds for interlayer slip. Finally, we perform an isothermal steady-state comparison to ablate the thermal cycling perturbation, isolating the contribution of dynamic structural relaxation from the baseline interfacial phonon scattering mechanism.
competitive_ideas.risks: ['1. Nanobeam electron diffraction may lack the spatial resolution or contrast to reliably detect sub-nanometer twist angle relaxation in the presence of complex thermal strain fields. Mitigation: Employ 4D-STEM with pixelated detectors to enhance strain and twist sensitivity.', '2. Thermal loading may induce irreversible chemical degradation (e.g., chalcogen vacancies, oxidation) rather than pure structural slip, confounding the observed drop in thermal conductivity. Mitigation: Perform all cycling in ultra-high vacuum and cross-validate with in situ Raman spectroscopy to distinguish chemical changes from moiré relaxation.', '3. Distinguishing the abrupt step-change of moiré slip from the continuous increase of Umklapp scattering may be obscured by measurement noise or spatial averaging. Mitigation: Use localized nanoscale thermal metrology (e.g., time-domain thermoreflectance with nanoscale resolution) to isolate the interface.']
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the target defects by replacing the static interfacial phonon scattering mechanism with the dynamic thermally-induced moiré lattice relaxation mechanism, directly addressing the unmapped target object. It sharpens the parent idea's thesis by establishing that the fundamental limit of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport is governed by structural stability boundaries under high power density, while the isothermal steady-state comparison isolates this mechanism to satisfy the direct observation evidence deficit.

competitive_ideas.abstract: High-power-density heat dissipation in twisted van der Waals heterostructures is fundamentally limited by interfacial thermal resistance, which is often modeled under the static assumption of twist-angle stability. Here, we replace the static twist-angle phonon scattering model with a thermally-induced twist-angle relaxation mechanism to explain thermal transport degradation under high power density. By correlating cross-plane time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with electron diffraction quantification before and after thermal cycling, we directly observe the structural relaxation of MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides. A thermal cycling ablation protocol isolates the contribution of twist-angle distribution perturbations from intrinsic phonon scattering, establishing critical binding energy thresholds where engineered thermal anisotropy fails.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy is bounded by a thermally-induced twist-angle relaxation mechanism, which dynamically degrades interfacial phonon transport under high power density, replacing the assumption of static twist-angle stability.
competitive_ideas.method: We realize the mechanism-commit-innovation by replacing the static_twist_angle_phonon_scattering_model with the thermally_induced_twist_angle_relaxation_mechanism. First, we characterize the thermal transport limit (cross-plane thermal conductivity) of the nanoscale thermal material system (twisted MoS2/WS2 and other TMDs) using cross_plane_thermal_conductivity_characterization via time-domain thermoreflectance. Next, we perturb the system by applying controlled thermal cycling to drive the thermally_induced_twist_angle_relaxation_mechanism. We then characterize the resulting structural changes by quantifying twist angle distribution shifts via electron diffraction, linking them to the degradation in the direct_thermal_observation signal. Finally, we execute the thermal_cycling_ablation_protocol by comparing thermally cycled samples against non-cycled controls and molecular dynamics predictions of critical binding energy thresholds, isolating the relaxation mechanism's contribution to the thermal transport limit.

competitive_ideas.title: Ultrafast Hot-Phonon Perturbation Reveals Transient Thermal Bottlenecks in Graphene/h-BN Heterostructures
competitive_ideas.abstract: Interfacial thermal resistance bottlenecks nanoscale heat dissipation, yet the fundamental limits under high power density are obscured by steady-state assumptions. We invert the premise that continuous strain-driven thermal feedback is required to probe these limits, committing instead to the hot-optical-phonon bottleneck as the primary transient mechanism. By replacing continuous closed-loop strain tuning with femtosecond optical pump-probe perturbation, we directly isolate the non-equilibrium hot-phonon decay rate across static Moiré interfacial registries in graphene/h-BN heterostructures. Using femtosecond transient thermoreflectance as precision thermal metrology, we establish the true thermal saturation ceiling, explicitly decoupling this from electron-phonon thermalization and acoustic phonon transmission limits. Cryogenic static bonding metrology confirms that the transient hot-phonon bottleneck, rather than steady-state phonon scattering or carrier cooling limits, dictates the high-power dissipation limit.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The conceptual repair is the inversion of steady-state, strain-driven thermal feedback into a femtosecond hot-phonon perturbation mechanism, enabling the direct observation of the transient thermal bottleneck that fundamentally limits high-power-density heat dissipation at atomic interfaces, while rigorously decoupling it from electron-phonon and acoustic phonon confounders.
competitive_ideas.method: We realize the conceptual move of ultrafast hot-phonon perturbation by replacing continuous dynamic strain tuning with discrete optical pump-probe sequences. First, we synthesize graphene/h-BN van der Waals heterostructures on a piezoelectric substrate and fix the atomic bonding configuration to specific Moiré superlattice registries via static piezoelectric strain actuation. Instead of continuous closed-loop feedback, we apply ultrafast optical pump pulses to directly perturb the hot-optical-phonon population at the interface. We then use ultrafast time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) as the precision thermal metrology to directly observe the hot-phonon decay rate and resolve the transient interfacial thermal resistance. To validate the mechanism-commit, we execute a cryogenic static bonding ablation, cooling the system to freeze lattice vibrations and holding the strain static, thereby isolating the hot-phonon bottleneck from steady-state phonon scattering pathways. Finally, we drive the heterostructure with high-power-density heat flux to bound the thermal saturation limits of the hot-phonon decay mechanism.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risks include the inability of standard thermoreflectance setups to achieve the sub-10 ps temporal resolution required for optical phonons, necessitating specialized femtosecond pump-probe configurations. Additionally, high pump fluence might induce non-linear thermal effects or damage the h-BN layer. There is also a risk that electron-phonon coupling in graphene is slower than expected, masking the optical phonon bottleneck. Mitigation involves strict fluence calibration, in-situ Raman mapping, and independent pump-probe measurements of the Dirac fermion cooling.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the evidence_role_deficit by replacing passive, steady-state strain feedback with an active, ultrafast perturbation mechanism that directly targets the direct_observation gap for transient thermal limits. By committing to the hot-phonon bottleneck mechanism and using cryogenic ablation to isolate it, the method explicitly bounds the thermal saturation limits under high power density, sharpening the parent idea's focus on fundamental heat transfer limits.

competitive_ideas.title: Direct Observation and Closed-Loop Engineering of Non-Equilibrium Hot Optical Phonon Scattering at Epitaxial Interfaces via Ultrafast Electron Diffraction
competitive_ideas.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat dissipation in nanoscale devices are bottlenecked by interfacial thermal resistance, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing non-equilibrium phonon scattering remain obscured by steady-state measurements and confounded by bulk thermalization. We introduce a representation shift from steady-state thermal diffusion to ultrafast transient dynamics, using momentum-resolved ultrafast electron diffraction (UED) to directly characterize hot optical phonon populations at GaN/AlN epitaxial thin-film interfaces. By decoupling optical phonons from coherent strain pulses and bounding pump fluence to isolate interfacial scattering from bulk electron-phonon thermalization, we iteratively perturb the interfacial structure via sub-monolayer ion-beam mixing. This isolates the specific non-equilibrium phonon scattering mechanisms that dictate thermal transport limits, providing the missing direct observation of interfacial thermal dynamics and establishing a new paradigm for precision thermal metrology.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Shifting the explanatory representation of interfacial heat transfer to momentum-resolved ultrafast transient phonon dynamics enables the direct characterization and iterative structural perturbation of non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering, explicitly decoupled from bulk electron-phonon thermalization and strain confounders, to isolate the atomic-scale bonding mechanisms governing thermal transport limits.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is a representation shift from steady-state thermal diffusion to non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering. We synthesize GaN/AlN epitaxial thin-film interfaces and apply interfacial bonding engineering via controlled sub-monolayer ion-beam mixing and annealing to tune atomic-scale defect states. We utilize ultrafast electron diffraction (UED) to directly observe the transient atomic displacements and hot optical phonon populations at the interface. The ultrafast electron diffraction phonon population feedback is rewired to dynamically execute a sub-monolayer ion beam mixing parameter update, iteratively minimizing non-equilibrium phonon scattering. To validate, we perform an unengineered baseline interface ablation, comparing the engineered interfaces against an unengineered baseline to isolate the interfacial scattering from bulk anharmonic decay. Finally, we conduct a high power density optical pump stress test to bound the thermal saturation limits and identify failure boundaries where irreversible defect generation occurs.
competitive_ideas.risks: The primary risk is that UED may lack sufficient momentum resolution to fully decouple electronic, acoustic strain, and phononic contributions to the diffraction signal, leading to ambiguous structural interpretations. Another risk is that ion-beam mixing may introduce deep-level defects that dominate scattering, masking the targeted bonding effects; this is bounded by strictly limiting the mixing energy to sub-monolayer perturbations. Finally, high-fluence optical pump pulses may induce non-thermal melting or shift the dominant decay pathway to bulk electron-phonon thermalization, bounded by monitoring the UED Debye-Waller factor and pump-fluence dependence.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the evidence_role_deficit by providing the required direct observation of atomic-scale interfacial bonding and thermal dynamics via ultrafast electron diffraction. By replacing the weak steady-state thermal diffusion representation with non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering and employing an unengineered baseline interface ablation, it sharpens the parent idea's thesis. The addition of the high power density optical pump stress test explicitly bounds the mechanism under worst-case conditions, ensuring the causal link between interfacial bonding and thermal transport limits is defensible and reproducible.

competitive_ideas.title: Strain-Tunable Phonon Transmission at Piezoelectrically Gated van der Waals Heterointerfaces: Revealing the Dynamic Phenomenon of Interfacial Thermal Conductance Modulation
competitive_ideas.abstract: Interfacial thermal boundary resistance (ITBR) is conventionally treated as a fixed material-pair property, fundamentally bottlenecking heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics. We invert this premise by demonstrating that ITBR is a dynamically tunable phenomenon governed by strain-mediated phonon transmission at the atomic interface. Using out-of-plane piezoelectric strain modulation of a graphene/hBN heterointerface on an AlN transduction layer, we directly alter the van der Waals interlayer spacing and thereby shift the cross-plane phonon density-of-states overlap governing interfacial transmission. Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) with sub-nanosecond resolution captures the conductance response under controlled bias, revealing a measurable phonon-transmission ceiling that shifts with the applied out-of-plane strain field. Crucially, by rigorously decoupling electro-optic thermoreflectance artifacts and in-plane thermal conductivity shifts, this establishes active interfacial thermal conductance modulation as a distinct, mechanism-resolved thermal transport phenomenon beyond static Kapitza resistance.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Thermal boundary conductance at van der Waals heterointerfaces is not a static material-pair invariant but a dynamically tunable phenomenon governed by out-of-plane strain-modulated van der Waals gap and cross-plane phonon density-of-states overlap; the fundamental limit on heat transfer across interfaces can therefore be actively shifted rather than merely accepted as a fixed Kapitza bottleneck, provided electro-optic and in-plane confounders are rigorously decoupled.
competitive_ideas.method: Conceptual move: Replace the assumption that interfacial thermal boundary resistance is a fixed, geometry-independent material property (static_kapitza_resistance_model) with the hypothesis that it is a strain-tunable phonon-transmission phenomenon (strain_tunable_phonon_transmission_mechanism). (1) Synthesize a graphene/hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) van der Waals heterostructure on a piezoelectric aluminum nitride (AlN) transduction layer, forming the atomic_scale_interface where heat transfer limits are evaluated. (2) Apply controllable in-plane strain via piezoelectric bias to the AlN layer, executing the interfacial_bond_tuning process that modifies the local bonding potential at the graphene/hBN interface. (3) Characterize the resulting interfacial_bonding_structure using cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) to confirm sub-angstrom bonding changes. (4) Perform precision_thermal_metrology via TDTR with sub-nanosecond temporal resolution under varying piezoelectric bias, measuring the thermal boundary conductance as a function of strain state. (5) Execute the zero_bias_ablation_protocol: repeat TDTR under zero-bias conditions with identical thermal loading to isolate strain-dependent conductance shifts from Joule heating and instrumental artifacts. (6) Compare measured conductance shifts against atomistic Green's function (AGF) simulations of phonon transmission spectra to identify the phonon_transmission_limit mechanism—specifically, which phonon frequency bands are activated or suppressed by the strain-modified bonding environment.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk: The measured thermal boundary conductance shows no statistically significant dependence on applied out-of-plane piezoelectric strain after decoupling artifacts. Mitigation: Use multiple heterointerface systems; employ zero_bias_ablation_protocol and electro-optic calibration. Secondary risk: Joule heating from the piezoelectric bias masks the strain-induced conductance change. Mitigation: Employ pulsed bias with thermal relaxation intervals. Tertiary risk: The van der Waals interface delaminates or slips under applied strain. Mitigation: Monitor interface integrity via in situ STEM and limit strain amplitude. Quaternary risk: In-plane strain alters lateral heat spreading. Mitigation: Use frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) to decouple cross-plane and in-plane thermal transport.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped_gap:phenomenon by identifying a concrete, mechanism-resolved phenomenon—active interfacial thermal conductance modulation via strain-tunable phonon transmission—that has been absent from the evidence cluster on atomic-scale interfacial bonding and precision thermal metrology. By replacing the static_kapitza_resistance_model with the strain_tunable_phonon_transmission_mechanism, the intervention shifts the parent idea from merely characterizing a fixed bottleneck to demonstrating a controllable thermal transport limit, directly addressing the high-power-density heat dissipation challenge in nanoscale electronics. The zero_bias_ablation_protocol isolates the mechanism from confounding artifacts, ensuring the phenomenon claim is falsifiable.
