competitive_ideas.abstract: The fundamental limits of heat transfer in twisted van der Waals heterostructures are constrained by the structural stability of the twist angle under high power density. We investigate the thermomechanical limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy by identifying the intrinsic critical binding energy threshold for interlayer sliding, which governs moiré phonon scattering and thermal saturation. By utilizing in-situ thermal and structural characterization during controlled thermal cycling, we precisely bound this threshold and isolate the phonon scattering boundaries prior to catastrophic delamination, while explicitly decoupling these effects from point defect generation and intrinsic Umklapp scattering. By measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity, twist angle distribution, and defect concentrations before and after thermal cycling, we validate the stability assumption across MoS2/WS2 and extend it to other transition metal dichalcogenides, resolving the unmapped phenomena of thermal saturation and structural degradation at the nanoscale.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The structural stability and thermal transport limits of twist-angle-engineered transition metal dichalcogenides under high power density are intrinsically governed by a material-specific critical binding energy threshold for interlayer sliding, which dictates the onset of phonon scattering and thermal saturation, and can be precisely bounded through in-situ nanoscale thermal and structural characterization during controlled thermal cycling, provided point defect generation and intrinsic scattering limits are decoupled.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to rewire the in-situ thermal and structural characterization to dynamically update the adaptive thermal cycling protocol based on the molecular dynamics-validated critical binding energy threshold. First, we synthesize the interfacial thermal material system comprising twisted MoS2/WS2 and extend the library to other transition metal dichalcogenides. We characterize the system using in_situ_thermal_and_structural_characterization (time-domain thermoreflectance and selected area electron diffraction) to measure the cross-plane thermal conductivity and twist angle distribution. This characterization feedback continuously updates the thermal cycling process condition, ensuring the applied power density is bounded by the molecular_dynamics_validated_critical_binding_energy_threshold for interlayer sliding. To isolate the contribution of this feedback-closed-loop and confirm defect-level lift, we perform a fixed_amplitude_thermal_cycling_ablation, comparing the adaptive feedback against a static protocol. Finally, we perturb the system via a high_power_density_thermal_stress_test to record the failure boundaries, ensuring the loop distinguishes true binding energy degradation from irreversible defect generation.

competitive_ideas.title: Dynamic Stability Boundaries of Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Heterostructures Under High Power Density
competitive_ideas.abstract: The fundamental limits of cross-plane thermal transport in twist-angle-engineered transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures are obscured by structural instability under high power density. We replace the static equilibrium phonon transport assumption with a dynamic Moiré superlattice relaxation mechanism, revealing that excess interfacial thermal saturation beyond the intrinsic anharmonic phonon scattering baseline is bounded by a critical interfacial shear strength threshold. By coupling high-power-density thermal characterization with an adaptive thermal cycling protocol guided by in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction, we isolate the structural relaxation from chemical degradation and intrinsic Umklapp scattering limits. This representation shift from static metrology to dynamic stability validation establishes the causal link between phonon-interlayer coupling and thermal transport ceilings in nanoscale electronic systems.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in TMD heterostructures is bounded by a critical interfacial shear strength threshold that governs the transition from coherent phonon transport to excess interfacial thermal saturation beyond the intrinsic Umklapp scattering baseline via dynamic Moiré superlattice relaxation under high power density.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is a representation shift from static thermal metrology to dynamic stability validation of the interfacial thermal state via an experimental feedback loop. We implement this by: (1) replacing the static equilibrium phonon transport model with the power-driven Moiré twist-angle relaxation mechanism; (2) utilizing pump-probe TDTR thermal characterization to measure cross-plane thermal conductivity; (3) rewiring the in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction to the adaptive thermal cycling protocol, where the structural readout of twist-angle distribution dictates the subsequent high-power-density loading steps to isolate the structural contribution from chemical degradation; (4) executing the structural relaxation isolation protocol to ablate the feedback loop, confirming that fixed-step cycling without structural feedback fails to isolate the mechanism; and (5) applying the extreme power density stress test to bound the material generality and identify the critical binding energy threshold where the interfacial thermal state saturates.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk is that high power density induces irreversible chemical degradation, interfacial blistering, or delamination rather than reversible twist-angle relaxation, confounding the phonon scattering mechanism. A secondary risk is that intrinsic anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering dominates the thermal saturation, masking the Moiré relaxation effect. These are mitigated by restricting the operational window below the TMD decomposition threshold, using in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction to continuously monitor for structural degradation, and establishing a robust intrinsic scattering baseline.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped phenomenon (thermal saturation limits) and target object (twisted TMD interfaces) by shifting the explanatory level from equilibrium thermal properties to non-equilibrium stability boundaries via an adaptive experimental loop. The structural relaxation isolation protocol explicitly links the high-power thermal readout to the structural state evolution, providing a defensible causal story for the limits of heat transfer in Moiré superlattices without introducing unrelated interface bonding or measurement isolation problems.

competitive_ideas.title: Feedback-Guided Twist-Angle Modulation and In-Situ Annealing to Bound Moiré-Mediated Interfacial Thermal Resistance
competitive_ideas.abstract: Heat dissipation in nanoscale electronics is bottlenecked by interfacial thermal boundary resistance, which classical spatially averaged models fail to predict at atomically sharp, twisted interfaces. We propose that interfacial phonon coupling, governed by the periodic moiré potential and local stacking registry, dictates cross-plane heat transfer when the lattice twist angle is precisely modulated in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers. By closing the loop between time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements and twist-angle modulation, we systematically tune the interfacial structural state to maximize phonon spectral overlap. We perform in-situ thermal annealing to ablate extrinsic defect and contaminant scattering, apply high-power-density optical pumping to stress-test fundamental thermal saturation limits, and utilize complementary phonon spectroscopy to decouple bulk and strain-induced effects. This work establishes the intrinsic limits of heat transfer at atomic-scale moiré interfaces under high power density, moving beyond classical diffuse mismatch approximations while rigorously bounding strain and bulk confounders.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The fundamental limit of cross-plane heat dissipation at atomically sharp moiré interfaces is governed by twist-angle-dependent local interfacial registry and phonon transmission mediated by the periodic moiré potential, distinct from twist-induced bulk phonon dispersion changes or local strain-field variations, and is isolated via closed-loop TDTR-guided twist modulation, in-situ annealing, and complementary phonon spectroscopy.
competitive_ideas.method: Conceptually, we replace the weak classical acoustic mismatch scattering model with the refined interfacial phonon coupling mechanism to describe heat transfer across the periodic moiré potential of twisted TMD heterobilayers. We synthesize twisted MoSe2/WSe2 heterobilayers and apply deterministic twist-angle modulation, guided by real-time time_domain_thermoreflectance interfacial thermal resistance readouts, to systematically alter the interfacial moiré structural state. To validate the mechanism and bound extrinsic scattering, we perform an in_situ_thermal_annealing ablation, comparing the thermal resistance of as-exfoliated versus annealed interfaces. Finally, we apply high_power_density_optical_pumping to stress-test the interface, identifying the failure boundary where intrinsic phonon coupling saturates or structural degradation occurs.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk is that interfacial thermal resistance is dominated by extrinsic defects, trapped moisture, or twist-dependent contaminant trapping rather than intrinsic phonon coupling. Mitigation involves rigorous in-situ thermal annealing and comparing as-exfoliated versus annealed interfaces. Secondary risk is that twist-induced local strain fields alter bulk phonon dispersion, confounding the interfacial transmission signal. Mitigation involves using complementary Raman/photoluminescence spectroscopy to monitor bulk phonon modes and ensure they remain unperturbed. Tertiary risk is that high-power-density optical pumping induces irreversible structural degradation before the intrinsic thermal saturation limit is reached. Mitigation involves correlating optical pump-probe thermal transients with structural integrity monitoring.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped target object gap by substituting the generic van der Waals heterostructure with a twisted transition metal dichalcogenide moiré superlattice, providing a precise, periodic atomic-scale interfacial bonding landscape. It sharpens the parent idea by committing to interfacial phonon coupling mediated by the moiré potential and introduces a closed-loop TDTR-guided twist modulation and in-situ annealing ablation to definitively bound extrinsic defect scattering and high-power failure boundaries.

competitive_ideas.title: Feedback-Controlled Thermal Saturation: Closing the Loop Between Precision Thermal Metrology and Adaptive Electrical Pumping to Reveal Hot Optical Phonon Limits in Graphene-Silicon Carbide Heterojunctions
competitive_ideas.abstract: The fundamental thermal saturation limit of nanoscale electronic interfaces under high power density is governed by non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering, but remains obscured when measurements are decoupled from process control. We close this gap by implementing a feedback loop between precision thermal metrology and adaptive electrical pumping, transforming the monolayer graphene-4H-silicon carbide heterojunction into a dynamically controlled target object. The feedback signal—interfacial thermal resistance trajectory—drives bounded updates to pulse width, duty cycle, and peak power density to establish the macroscopic thermal saturation ceiling. To isolate the specific contribution of hot optical phonon accumulation to this ceiling, we employ isotopic perturbation (12C vs 13C graphene) and decouple its effect on the full phonon spectrum by comparing the macroscopic saturation trajectory against the theoretically bounded acoustic phonon transport limit. This representation shift resolves the unmapped target object gap and provides a falsifiable framework for ultimate heat dissipation limits.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The thermal saturation ceiling of nanoscale electronic interfaces is established through a closed-loop representation shift: coupling precision thermal metrology to adaptive electrical pumping defines the macroscopic stability boundary, while isotopic perturbation, decoupled from the acoustic phonon baseline, isolates the non-equilibrium hot optical phonon scattering mechanism governing this limit.
competitive_ideas.method: First, synthesize a monolayer graphene-4H-silicon carbide heterojunction with controlled covalent-van der Waals hybrid bonding. Second, deploy precision thermal metrology via time-domain thermoreflectance under electrical pumping to continuously characterize the interfacial thermal resistance, providing the characterization feedback signal. Third, implement an adaptive controller that adjusts the adaptive electrical pumping protocol based on the measured thermal resistance trajectory—increasing power when resistance remains stable and reducing power when resistance rises sharply. Fourth, ablate the hot optical phonon contribution via isotopic perturbation ablation (13C-enriched graphene vs natural 12C), comparing the feedback-controlled thermal saturation behavior. Fifth, execute a high power density stress test by pushing peak power density beyond the saturation threshold to identify the failure boundary where adaptive control can no longer suppress thermal runaway.

Mitigation: Implement cycle-to-cycle adaptation rather than real-time intra-pulse control, using rolling thermal resistance averages to establish the macroscopic boundary.', 'Secondary risk: Device degradation under sustained high power density may conflate irreversible damage with reversible hot phonon accumulation. Mitigation: Use ultra-short pulsed pumping with low duty cycle and cross-validate interface integrity via post-stress Raman spectroscopy.', 'Tertiary risk: Theoretical bounding of acoustic phonon mass-disorder scattering may carry significant uncertainty, obscuring the isolation of the optical phonon bottleneck. Mitigation: Cross-validate the acoustic baseline with non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations that separately resolve optical and acoustic phonon contributions.']
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the unmapped target object gap by explicitly defining the monolayer graphene-4H-silicon carbide heterojunction under active feedback control as the concrete target material system. By closing the loop between precision thermal metrology and adaptive electrical pumping, the thermal saturation ceiling becomes a directly observable and controllable property, making the non-equilibrium hot optical phonon mechanism falsifiable through systematic perturbation and bounded stress testing.

competitive_ideas.title: Structural Stability Boundaries of Strain-Tuned Moiré Thermal Transport in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
competitive_ideas.abstract: Dynamic modulation of the moiré potential landscape via mechanical strain offers a pathway to actively tune cross-plane thermal conductivity for adaptive thermal management. However, the structural stability of twisted interfaces under dynamic strain and the decoupling of moiré effects from intralayer phonon shifts remain unresolved. We propose that strain-tuned phonon transport in twisted van der Waals heterostructures is strictly bounded by critical interlayer sliding energy barriers. By correlating in situ cross-plane thermal conductivity with local interlayer registry changes via electron diffraction during strain application, and isolating the moiré-specific modulation from intralayer phonon dispersion shifts using untwisted reference heterostructures, we establish the material-dependent stability limits of moiré thermal transport. Extending this validation across transition metal dichalcogenides defines the fundamental operational boundaries for adaptive twist-angle thermal engineering.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: The causal link between dynamically applied mechanical strain and cross-plane thermal conductivity is bounded by the structural stability of the moiré superlattice, defined by critical interlayer sliding energy barriers, while the moiré-specific thermal modulation is isolated from confounding intralayer phonon dispersion changes.
competitive_ideas.method: We perturb twisted MoS2/WS2 heterostructures with controlled biaxial strain while measuring cross-plane thermal conductivity. To isolate the stability boundary using the thermal_cycling_and_electron_diffraction_ablation protocol, we subject the systems to thermal cycling and characterize the twist-angle distribution changes using ultrafast electron diffraction. We compare these experimental observations to molecular dynamics simulations to determine the critical binding energy thresholds for structural relaxation, replacing the assumption of static_twist_angle_phonon_scattering with strain_tuned_phonon_transport_with_structural_stability_bound. Finally, we extend this characterization to other transition metal dichalcogenides to bound the material generality of the mechanism.
competitive_ideas.risks: Risk of irreversible interlayer sliding or delamination during strain application. Risk that the moiré-specific thermal modulation is negligible compared to the intralayer phonon dispersion shifts, making it experimentally indistinguishable without extreme precision. Mitigation involves using molecular dynamics to identify the critical sliding energy barrier and the expected moiré-tuning magnitude beforehand.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This refinement resolves the missing boundary condition and measurement construct mismatch by explicitly defining the structural stability limits of the moiré potential under thermal and mechanical perturbations. By validating the causal link between strain and thermal conductivity against structural relaxation, it ensures the mechanism remains physically grounded and reproducible across different transition metal dichalcogenides.

competitive_ideas.expected_mechanism: Dynamic mechanical strain alters the local interlayer registry within the moiré superlattice, modulating cross-plane phonon transmission. However, this mechanism is constrained by the lateral corrugation of the interlayer potential energy surface; if the strain energy exceeds the critical sliding barrier, the layers undergo irreversible interlayer sliding. Concurrently, the strain alters the intralayer lattice constant, modifying the phonon dispersion; the true moiré-tuning mechanism is only confirmed when the thermal conductivity modulation exceeds the baseline shift observed in untwisted heterostructures.
competitive_ideas.discriminating_observation: Correlate the in situ cross-plane thermal conductivity with the local interlayer registry (moiré period) measured via electron diffraction before and after strain application, while comparing against untwisted (aligned) heterostructures subjected to identical strain to isolate the moiré-specific thermal modulation from the baseline intralayer phonon dispersion shifts. A divergence between the expected strain-tuned conductivity and the measured conductivity in the twisted sample, coincident with a shift in the electron diffraction moiré peaks and exceeding the untwisted baseline, discriminates elastic registry modulation from irreversible interlayer sliding and intralayer confounding.
competitive_ideas.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim fails if the moiré period remains perfectly stable despite strain exceeding the predicted sliding barrier, if the thermal conductivity changes are entirely uncorrelated with the local interlayer registry, or if the thermal conductivity modulation in the twisted structure is entirely accounted for by the changes observed in the untwisted structure, indicating no moiré-specific tuning.

evaluation.fairness_protocol: The proposal uses molecular dynamics to predict the critical binding energy threshold and restricts thermal cycling amplitude to the elastic regime, providing a theoretical baseline. However, a direct experimental comparator (e.g., an untwisted or statically twisted control under identical strain/thermal cycling) is needed to isolate the dynamic moiré effect from general strain-induced thermal changes in 2D materials.
evaluation.feedback: The proposal successfully introduces a critical boundary condition (structural stability bound) to the strain-tuned moiré thermal transport mechanism, addressing the missing boundary condition and unsupported causal link defects. However, the experimental feasibility of simultaneously applying biaxial strain, performing in situ cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements, and conducting ultrafast electron diffraction during thermal cycling is extremely low. The measurement construct mismatch risk remains high, as cross-plane thermal measurements in 2D heterostructures are notoriously susceptible to contact resistance and parasitic heat leaks, which could confound the attribution of thermal changes to moiré potential modulation. To improve feasibility and identifiability, the protocol should explicitly include a statically twisted control under identical strain and thermal cycling to decouple general strain effects from dynamic moiré modulation.
evaluation.defect_fix_summary: The mechanism-commit-innovation skill successfully addressed the missing_boundary_condition and unsupported_causal_link defects by explicitly defining the physical limits (critical interfacial binding energy thresholds) under which the strain-tuning mechanism remains valid. The addition of the thermal cycling and electron diffraction ablation protocol addresses the measurement_construct_mismatch and validation_gap defects by providing a concrete method to isolate the structural stability variable and confirm that observed thermal changes are due to moiré modulation rather than structural degradation.

competitive_ideas.title: Thermally Activated Interfacial Shear Creep and Stability Boundaries in Twist-Angle-Engineered van der Waals Heterostructures
competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered van der Waals heterostructures offer tunable thermal transport, but their operational limits are constrained by structural relaxation under thermal load. Moving beyond classical bulk phase transformation kinetics, we identify thermally activated interfacial shear creep mediated by moiré domain wall (soliton) glide as the fundamental mechanism governing twist-angle stability, provided interfacial delamination and chemical degradation are negligible. By applying controlled isothermal annealing and thermal cycling to MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides, we map the critical temperature-time boundaries where interfacial soliton glide initiates. Electron diffraction and cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements validate the structural and thermal degradation, while molecular dynamics determine the critical Peierls-like energy thresholds for domain wall motion. This establishes a predictive creep-based stability boundary for high-power-density thermal management, explicitly distinguishing soliton glide from point-defect slip and thermal expansion-induced delamination.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Replacing classical phase transformation kinetics with a mechanism of thermally activated interfacial shear creep mediated by moiré domain wall (soliton) glide to define the fundamental stability boundaries of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport, bounded against confounding delamination and chemical degradation.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move replaces discrete classical phase transformation kinetics with continuous thermally activated interfacial shear creep. We subject twisted_van_der_waals_heterostructures (MoS2/WS2 and other TMDs) to a temperature_time_thermal_protocol (isothermal anneals and thermal cycling). We characterize the twist_angle_stability_state via nanobeam electron diffraction to quantify moiré pattern degradation. Cross-plane thermal conductivity is measured before and after to link structural creep to thermal performance. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the activation energy for interfacial shear slip, establishing the interfacial_twist_relaxation_mechanism. Finally, we bound the stability_phase_diagram_boundary by identifying the critical temperature-time combinations where shear creep exceeds the moiré potential corrugation. To isolate the mechanism, we perform a spatial_moiré_pattern_ablation using high-resolution nanobeam electron diffraction to distinguish continuous uniform slip from localized nucleation and growth.
competitive_ideas.risks: The primary risk is that twist relaxation is dominated by static edge pinning, point-defect slip, or thermal expansion-induced delamination rather than interfacial soliton glide. Mitigation involves high-resolution spatial mapping of the moiré pattern and interfacial conformality via nanobeam electron diffraction to directly observe domain wall motion and rule out delamination. A secondary risk is that molecular dynamics simulations fail to capture the correct timescales for soliton glide, mitigated by cross-validation with experimental activation energies.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing an inappropriate metallurgical phase-transformation model with a physically accurate atomistic mechanism (interfacial shear creep) for 2D materials. It sharpens the parent idea by providing a mechanistically valid framework for predicting the operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal interfaces under high-power-density conditions.

competitive_ideas.title: Time-Temperature-Transformation Stability Boundaries for Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in van der Waals Heterostructures
competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in van der Waals heterostructures assumes structural stability under high-power-density operation, yet single-point thermal validations fail to capture time-dependent relaxation and often conflate it with defect-mediated phonon scattering or interfacial delamination. We introduce a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) stability boundary for twist angles, mapping the critical temperature-time combinations where the interfacial twist angle remains preserved versus relaxes. By replacing single-point thermal validation with a continuous stability phase diagram, we establish a predictive framework for the operational limits of twist-angle-engineered heat dissipation. We validate this boundary by correlating cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation with electron diffraction quantification of twist angle relaxation across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides, while explicitly decoupling these effects from thermally generated point defects and interfacial delamination using Raman spectroscopy and cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy, bounded by molecular dynamics-derived critical binding energy thresholds.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: We replace the single-point thermal validation of twist-angle stability with a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) stability boundary, providing a predictive phase diagram that discriminates between preserved and relaxed interfacial twist angles under high-power-density thermal loads. This resolves the measurement construct mismatch in twist-angle-engineered thermal transport by explicitly decoupling true twist angle relaxation from confounding mechanisms such as point defect generation and interfacial delamination.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to treat twist-angle relaxation not as a binary pass/fail at a single temperature, but as a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) process analogous to metallurgical phase kinetics. First, we synthesize twisted_van_der_waals_heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/WS2 and extended to other TMDs) with controlled interfacial twist angles. Second, we apply a temperature_time_annealing_protocol across a matrix of temperatures and isothermal hold times to perturb the system. Third, we characterize the twist_angle_relaxation_state using nanobeam electron diffraction to quantify the distribution of twist angles, and measure the cross-plane thermal conductivity as the property endpoint. Fourth, we construct the stability_phase_diagram by bounding the critical temperature-time combinations where the twist angle degrades, validated against molecular dynamics simulations of the thermal_relaxation_mechanism and critical binding energy thresholds. Finally, we execute an isothermal_ablation_protocol to isolate the contribution of the time-transformation boundary from simple temperature-driven degradation.
competitive_ideas.risks: The primary risk is that the twist angle relaxation mechanism is purely temperature-driven (athermal) rather than time-dependent. Another risk is that defect generation or delamination kinetics overlap with the TTT boundary, making it impossible to decouple the twist angle relaxation mechanism from these confounders using the proposed characterization suite.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This application of mechanism-commit-innovation resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing a weak, single-point thermal validation with a refined time-temperature-transformation stability boundary. It sharpens the parent idea's thesis by providing a predictive, mechanistic framework for the operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy, directly addressing the missing boundary condition in high-power-density heat dissipation.

competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle engineering in van der Waals heterostructures promises tunable cross-plane thermal conductivity, but its operational limits under high-power-density thermal cycling remain unbounded due to structural relaxation artifacts. We replace empirical discrete thermal cycling tests with a Time-Temperature-Relaxation (TTR) kinetic boundary—a TTT-analogous framework adapted for structural evolution—to map the critical limits of twist-angle relaxation. By integrating nanodiffraction-based twist angle quantification, cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements, and molecular dynamics-derived binding energy thresholds across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides, we establish a predictive framework for structural stability. This mechanism-commit replaces isolated thermal stress tests with a continuous stability boundary, directly contextualizing measurement artifacts by decoupling intrinsic phonon scattering limits from structural evolution artifacts, while explicitly controlling for substrate strain relaxation and defect-generation confounders.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: We introduce a Time-Temperature-Relaxation (TTR) kinetic boundary as a refined structural boundary condition, replacing discrete thermal cycling tests to predictively map the twist-angle relaxation mechanism and operational thermal limits in van der Waals heterostructures, explicitly isolating interlayer sliding from substrate strain and defect-mediated degradation.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is substituting discrete_thermal_cycling_tests with a continuous TTT_stability_phase_diagram that maps the twist-angle relaxation mechanism as a function of temperature, time, and interlayer binding energy. Concretely, we synthesize twisted MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures. We perturb these systems using controlled temperature-time thermal cycling. We characterize the twist angle distribution changes via nanobeam electron diffraction and measure cross-plane thermal conductivity using time-domain thermoreflectance. We compare these experimental observations against molecular dynamics simulations to determine critical binding energy thresholds. We validate this kinetic framework by correlating twist-angle distribution changes with cross-plane thermal conductivity, determining critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics, and extending the stability phase diagram across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides. Crucially, we isolate pure rotational slip from confounding in-plane translational sliding, defect-mediated relaxation, and thermal expansion-induced delamination. This representation shift exposes the activation barrier invariant for interfacial slip, providing a predictive boundary for twist-angle engineering.

competitive_ideas.title: Time-Temperature-Transformation Stability Diagrams for Twist-Angle Engineering in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
competitive_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal transport in van der Waals heterostructures assumes structural stability of the moiré configuration under thermal load, but this assumption lacks a predictive stability boundary. We apply time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram methodology as a phenomenological framework to map the critical temperature-time combinations where twist angles remain fixed versus undergo interfacial rotational relaxation in MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures. By systematically annealing heterostructures across isothermal conditions and quantifying twist angle distributions via selected area electron diffraction alongside cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements, we construct a stability phase diagram. We test the hypothesis that if relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, it will trace a characteristic nose curve where thermal activation of rotational relaxation is fastest. This provides a predictive framework for operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport, linking structural relaxation kinetics to moiré-periodicity-dependent phonon scattering.
competitive_ideas.core_contribution: Twist-angle stability in van der Waals heterostructures can be mapped to time-temperature-transformation kinetics: if interfacial rotational relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, it traces a characteristic nose curve in temperature-time space, defining a phenomenological stability phase diagram that bounds the operational envelope for twist-angle-engineered cross-plane thermal transport governed by moiré phonon scattering.
competitive_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to transfer TTT diagram construction from metallurgical phase transformations to twist-angle structural stability in 2D heterostructures, treating interfacial rotational relaxation as the transformation event. (1) Synthesize MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 twisted bilayer heterostructures with controlled initial twist angles (0°–5°) via dry transfer. (2) Subject heterostructures to isothermal annealing across temperatures 150°C–500°C with hold times from 1 minute to 100 hours, constituting the temperature_time_thermal_cycling matrix. (3) Characterize twist_angle_stability_state via selected area electron diffraction before and after each annealing condition, quantifying the twist angle distribution width and mean shift. (4) Measure cross-plane thermal conductivity using time-domain thermoreflectance before and after annealing to correlate structural relaxation with property_or_performance_endpoint changes. (5) Perform molecular dynamics simulations to compute activation energy barriers for interfacial_rotational_relaxation and predict TTT boundary positions. (6) Construct the stability_phase_diagram plotting critical time versus temperature, identifying the nose temperature where relaxation is fastest. (7) Extend validation to additional TMD combinations to test material generality of the TTT framework.
competitive_ideas.risks: Primary risk: relaxation follows uniform sliding over a single barrier, yielding simple Arrhenius kinetics and falsifying the TTT nose curve hypothesis. Secondary risk: thermal conductivity changes are dominated by defect generation rather than moiré phonon scattering.
competitive_ideas.rationale: This mechanism-commit-innovation resolves measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing the implicit assumption of fixed twist angles with an explicit, quantifiable interfacial rotational relaxation mechanism bounded by temperature-time conditions. It addresses missing_boundary_condition by constructing the TTT stability phase diagram that defines where twist-angle-engineered thermal transport claims remain valid. The verification reversal route ensures the mechanism is back-inferred from observable twist angle distribution changes and thermal conductivity degradation, with pre-registered competing kinetic predictions.

hypothesis_contract.expected_mechanism: Thermal activation provides energy to overcome the interfacial rotational energy barrier between moiré configurations, causing layers to rotate toward lower-energy commensurate angles. high_risk_ideas.title: Thermally Activated Interfacial Shear Creep and Stability Boundaries in Twist-Angle-Engineered van der Waals Heterostructures
high_risk_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered van der Waals heterostructures offer tunable thermal transport, but their operational limits are constrained by structural relaxation under thermal load. Moving beyond classical bulk phase transformation kinetics, we identify thermally activated interfacial shear creep mediated by moiré domain wall (soliton) glide as the fundamental mechanism governing twist-angle stability, provided interfacial delamination and chemical degradation are negligible. By applying controlled isothermal annealing and thermal cycling to MoS2/WS2 and other transition metal dichalcogenides, we map the critical temperature-time boundaries where interfacial soliton glide initiates. Electron diffraction and cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements validate the structural and thermal degradation, while molecular dynamics determine the critical Peierls-like energy thresholds for domain wall motion. This establishes a predictive creep-based stability boundary for high-power-density thermal management, explicitly distinguishing soliton glide from point-defect slip and thermal expansion-induced delamination.
high_risk_ideas.core_contribution: Replacing classical phase transformation kinetics with a mechanism of thermally activated interfacial shear creep mediated by moiré domain wall (soliton) glide to define the fundamental stability boundaries of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport, bounded against confounding delamination and chemical degradation.
high_risk_ideas.method: The conceptual move replaces discrete classical phase transformation kinetics with continuous thermally activated interfacial shear creep. We subject twisted_van_der_waals_heterostructures (MoS2/WS2 and other TMDs) to a temperature_time_thermal_protocol (isothermal anneals and thermal cycling). We characterize the twist_angle_stability_state via nanobeam electron diffraction to quantify moiré pattern degradation. Cross-plane thermal conductivity is measured before and after to link structural creep to thermal performance. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the activation energy for interfacial shear slip, establishing the interfacial_twist_relaxation_mechanism. Finally, we bound the stability_phase_diagram_boundary by identifying the critical temperature-time combinations where shear creep exceeds the moiré potential corrugation. To isolate the mechanism, we perform a spatial_moiré_pattern_ablation using high-resolution nanobeam electron diffraction to distinguish continuous uniform slip from localized nucleation and growth.
high_risk_ideas.risks: The primary risk is that twist relaxation is dominated by static edge pinning, point-defect slip, or thermal expansion-induced delamination rather than interfacial soliton glide. Mitigation involves high-resolution spatial mapping of the moiré pattern and interfacial conformality via nanobeam electron diffraction to directly observe domain wall motion and rule out delamination. A secondary risk is that molecular dynamics simulations fail to capture the correct timescales for soliton glide, mitigated by cross-validation with experimental activation energies.
high_risk_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing an inappropriate metallurgical phase-transformation model with a physically accurate atomistic mechanism (interfacial shear creep) for 2D materials. It sharpens the parent idea by providing a mechanistically valid framework for predicting the operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal interfaces under high-power-density conditions.

high_risk_ideas.title: Time-Temperature-Transformation Stability Boundaries for Twist-Angle-Engineered Thermal Anisotropy in van der Waals Heterostructures
high_risk_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in van der Waals heterostructures assumes structural stability under high-power-density operation, yet single-point thermal validations fail to capture time-dependent relaxation and often conflate it with defect-mediated phonon scattering or interfacial delamination. We introduce a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) stability boundary for twist angles, mapping the critical temperature-time combinations where the interfacial twist angle remains preserved versus relaxes. By replacing single-point thermal validation with a continuous stability phase diagram, we establish a predictive framework for the operational limits of twist-angle-engineered heat dissipation. We validate this boundary by correlating cross-plane thermal conductivity degradation with electron diffraction quantification of twist angle relaxation across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides, while explicitly decoupling these effects from thermally generated point defects and interfacial delamination using Raman spectroscopy and cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy, bounded by molecular dynamics-derived critical binding energy thresholds.
high_risk_ideas.core_contribution: We replace the single-point thermal validation of twist-angle stability with a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) stability boundary, providing a predictive phase diagram that discriminates between preserved and relaxed interfacial twist angles under high-power-density thermal loads. This resolves the measurement construct mismatch in twist-angle-engineered thermal transport by explicitly decoupling true twist angle relaxation from confounding mechanisms such as point defect generation and interfacial delamination.
high_risk_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to treat twist-angle relaxation not as a binary pass/fail at a single temperature, but as a time-temperature-transformation (TTT) process analogous to metallurgical phase kinetics. First, we synthesize twisted_van_der_waals_heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/WS2 and extended to other TMDs) with controlled interfacial twist angles. Second, we apply a temperature_time_annealing_protocol across a matrix of temperatures and isothermal hold times to perturb the system. Third, we characterize the twist_angle_relaxation_state using nanobeam electron diffraction to quantify the distribution of twist angles, and measure the cross-plane thermal conductivity as the property endpoint. Fourth, we construct the stability_phase_diagram by bounding the critical temperature-time combinations where the twist angle degrades, validated against molecular dynamics simulations of the thermal_relaxation_mechanism and critical binding energy thresholds. Finally, we execute an isothermal_ablation_protocol to isolate the contribution of the time-transformation boundary from simple temperature-driven degradation.
high_risk_ideas.risks: The primary risk is that the twist angle relaxation mechanism is purely temperature-driven (athermal) rather than time-dependent. Another risk is that defect generation or delamination kinetics overlap with the TTT boundary, making it impossible to decouple the twist angle relaxation mechanism from these confounders using the proposed characterization suite.
high_risk_ideas.rationale: This application of mechanism-commit-innovation resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing a weak, single-point thermal validation with a refined time-temperature-transformation stability boundary. It sharpens the parent idea's thesis by providing a predictive, mechanistic framework for the operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy, directly addressing the missing boundary condition in high-power-density heat dissipation.

high_risk_ideas.title: Kinetic Time-Temperature-Transformation Mapping of Interfacial Rotational Slip in Twisted van der Waals Heterostructures
high_risk_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered van der Waals heterostructures offer tunable thermal transport, but operational stability under high power density is limited by interfacial relaxation. We replace the assumption of a static thermodynamic stability threshold with a kinetic time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram to resolve measurement construct mismatches in predicting structural relaxation. By closing the loop between in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction and adaptive thermal cycling, we map critical temperature-time combinations where twist angles remain stable versus relax. We validate this kinetic framework by correlating twist-angle distribution changes with cross-plane thermal conductivity, determining critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics, and extending the stability phase diagram across multiple transition metal dichalcogenides. Crucially, we isolate pure rotational slip from confounding in-plane translational sliding, defect-mediated relaxation, and thermal expansion-induced delamination. This representation shift exposes the activation barrier invariant for interfacial slip, providing a predictive boundary for twist-angle engineering.
high_risk_ideas.core_contribution: Shifting the representation of twist-angle stability from a static thermodynamic threshold to a kinetic time-temperature-transformation diagram exposes the time-temperature invariant of interfacial rotational slip, resolving measurement construct mismatches while explicitly isolating rotational slip from in-plane translational sliding, defect-mediated relaxation, and delamination.
high_risk_ideas.method: We realize the representation shift by replacing the static_thermodynamic_stability_threshold with the kinetic_time_temperature_transformation_diagram. First, we synthesize twisted van der Waals heterostructures (e.g., MoS2/WS2, MoSe2/WSe2). Instead of a brute-force static grid, we apply an adaptive temperature_time_thermal_cycling protocol driven by real-time feedback from in-situ nanobeam electron diffraction to track the twist_angle_structural_state. This rapidly converges on the kinetic boundary of interfacial_rotational_slip. We characterize the structural state and measure the cross-plane thermal conductivity before and after cycling to link the structural relaxation to the thermal property endpoint. We construct the kinetic_time_temperature_transformation_diagram from this adaptive sampling and determine critical binding energy thresholds via molecular dynamics validated against the experimental TTT boundaries. To isolate the contribution of the representation shift and confirm the lift on measurement_construct_mismatch, we perform a static_grid_thermal_cycling_ablation, comparing the boundary resolution and efficiency against the adaptive kinetic protocol.
high_risk_ideas.risks: ['1. Twist-angle relaxation may be purely thermodynamic (instantaneous at a critical temperature) rather than kinetic, falsifying the TTT representation. Mitigation: The static_grid_thermal_cycling_ablation will reveal if the time-axis is meaningful; if relaxation is instantaneous, the TTT diagram will collapse to a single vertical line.', '2. Interfacial rotational slip may not be the dominant relaxation mechanism; in-plane layer sliding or defect-mediated relaxation could dominate. Mitigation: Cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements and nanobeam diffraction symmetry analysis will be used to discriminate between slip mechanisms based on their distinct structural and thermal signatures.', '3. Thermal expansion mismatch may induce delamination, altering cross-plane thermal conductivity without interfacial slip. Mitigation: Thickness-profile and diffraction intensity tracking will be used to bound the delamination regime and exclude it from the rotational slip TTT mapping.']
high_risk_ideas.rationale: This skill application resolves the measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing a static thermodynamic threshold with a kinetic state-space representation (TTT diagram). It sharpens the parent idea's thesis by explicitly defining the invariant (activation barrier for interfacial rotational slip) and providing an efficient, predictive framework for operational stability boundaries in high-power-density thermal transport, validated across material families and linked to thermal property endpoints.

high_risk_ideas.title: Time-Temperature-Transformation Stability Diagrams for Twist-Angle Engineering in Van Der Waals Heterostructures
high_risk_ideas.abstract: Twist-angle-engineered thermal transport in van der Waals heterostructures assumes structural stability of the moiré configuration under thermal load, but this assumption lacks a predictive stability boundary. We apply time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram methodology as a phenomenological framework to map the critical temperature-time combinations where twist angles remain fixed versus undergo interfacial rotational relaxation in MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures. By systematically annealing heterostructures across isothermal conditions and quantifying twist angle distributions via selected area electron diffraction alongside cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements, we construct a stability phase diagram. We test the hypothesis that if relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, it will trace a characteristic nose curve where thermal activation of rotational relaxation is fastest. This provides a predictive framework for operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered thermal transport, linking structural relaxation kinetics to moiré-periodicity-dependent phonon scattering.
high_risk_ideas.core_contribution: Twist-angle stability in van der Waals heterostructures can be mapped to time-temperature-transformation kinetics: if interfacial rotational relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, it traces a characteristic nose curve in temperature-time space, defining a phenomenological stability phase diagram that bounds the operational envelope for twist-angle-engineered cross-plane thermal transport governed by moiré phonon scattering.
high_risk_ideas.method: The conceptual move is to transfer TTT diagram construction from metallurgical phase transformations to twist-angle structural stability in 2D heterostructures, treating interfacial rotational relaxation as the transformation event. (1) Synthesize MoS2/WS2 and MoSe2/WSe2 twisted bilayer heterostructures with controlled initial twist angles (0°–5°) via dry transfer. (2) Subject heterostructures to isothermal annealing across temperatures 150°C–500°C with hold times from 1 minute to 100 hours, constituting the temperature_time_thermal_cycling matrix. (3) Characterize twist_angle_stability_state via selected area electron diffraction before and after each annealing condition, quantifying the twist angle distribution width and mean shift. (4) Measure cross-plane thermal conductivity using time-domain thermoreflectance before and after annealing to correlate structural relaxation with property_or_performance_endpoint changes. (5) Perform molecular dynamics simulations to compute activation energy barriers for interfacial_rotational_relaxation and predict TTT boundary positions. (6) Construct the stability_phase_diagram plotting critical time versus temperature, identifying the nose temperature where relaxation is fastest. (7) Extend validation to additional TMD combinations to test material generality of the TTT framework.
high_risk_ideas.risks: Primary risk: relaxation follows uniform sliding over a single barrier, yielding simple Arrhenius kinetics and falsifying the TTT nose curve hypothesis. Secondary risk: thermal conductivity changes are dominated by defect generation rather than moiré phonon scattering.
high_risk_ideas.rationale: This mechanism-commit-innovation resolves measurement_construct_mismatch by replacing the implicit assumption of fixed twist angles with an explicit, quantifiable interfacial rotational relaxation mechanism bounded by temperature-time conditions. It addresses missing_boundary_condition by constructing the TTT stability phase diagram that defines where twist-angle-engineered thermal transport claims remain valid. The verification reversal route ensures the mechanism is back-inferred from observable twist angle distribution changes and thermal conductivity degradation, with pre-registered competing kinetic predictions.

hypothesis_contract.central_hypothesis: The twist_angle_stability_state in transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures follows time-temperature-transformation kinetics, where interfacial_rotational_relaxation exhibits a characteristic nose curve in temperature-time space, such that cross-plane thermal conductivity degrades predictably when the twist angle exceeds a critical relaxation threshold defined by the stability_phase_diagram boundary.
hypothesis_contract.mechanism_or_relation: interfacial_rotational_relaxation driven by thermal activation following TTT kinetics with characteristic nose curve in temperature-time space
hypothesis_contract.intervention_or_transformation: Systematic isothermal annealing of twisted_vdw_heterostructures across a temperature-time matrix (150°C–500°C, 1 min–100 hrs) to perturb the twist_angle_stability_state and activate interfacial_rotational_relaxation, with characterization before and after to construct the stability_phase_diagram.
hypothesis_contract.expected_mechanism: Thermal activation provides energy to overcome the interfacial rotational energy barrier between moiré configurations, causing layers to rotate toward lower-energy commensurate angles. The relaxation rate follows Arrhenius kinetics with a nucleation-limited regime at lower temperatures and diffusion-limited regime at higher temperatures, producing the characteristic TTT nose curve where relaxation time is minimized at an intermediate temperature.
hypothesis_contract.discriminating_observation: The stability_phase_diagram must exhibit a characteristic nose curve shape where the critical time for twist angle relaxation reaches a minimum at an intermediate temperature (predicted 250°C–350°C for MoS2/WS2), and the twist angle distribution width must correlate with cross-plane thermal conductivity reduction (>15% decrease when twist angle shifts >1°). Competing mechanisms (monotonic relaxation, pure threshold behavior, defect-dominated conductivity changes) are falsified if they cannot reproduce both the nose curve shape and the structure-property correlation.
hypothesis_contract.boundary_or_failure_condition: The TTT stability framework fails if: (1) twist angle distributions show no measurable change across all temperature-time conditions, indicating stability beyond the probed range; (2) the relaxation kinetics do not exhibit a nose curve but instead follow monotonic or threshold behavior; (3) cross-plane thermal conductivity changes are uncorrelated with twist angle distribution shifts; (4) the framework does not transfer to MoSe2/WSe2 or other TMD combinations with different interfacial binding energies.
hypothesis_contract.evidence_requirement: Selected area electron diffraction patterns quantifying twist angle distributions across the full temperature-time matrix showing systematic evolution; cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements before and after annealing demonstrating correlation with twist angle relaxation; molecular dynamics predictions of activation energy barriers that match experimentally determined TTT boundary positions; extension to at least one additional TMD heterostructure system confirming material generality.

hypothesis_contract.claim_scope: Valid for transition metal dichalcogenide twisted bilayer heterostructures with twist angles 0°–5° under isothermal annealing conditions 150°C–500°C; predictive framework for operational stability limits of twist-angle-engineered cross-plane thermal transport in nanometre-scale electronic devices.
hypothesis_contract.assumptions: Twist angle relaxation follows classical nucleation-and-growth kinetics analogous to metallurgical phase transformations; interfacial rotational energy barriers are well-defined and thermally activatable; electron diffraction can resolve twist angle changes >0.5°; cross-plane thermal conductivity is sensitive to moiré configuration changes.
hypothesis_contract.gap_alignment: The TTT stability phase diagram directly addresses the gap in identifying fundamental and material-dependent limits on thermal transport by providing a predictive boundary condition for when twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy remains stable versus relaxes under thermal load, defining the operational limits of heat dissipation in nanometre-scale electronic devices.
hypothesis_contract.evidence_basis: Selected area electron diffraction patterns across temperature-time matrix; time-domain thermoreflectance cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements; molecular dynamics activation energy calculations; Raman spectroscopy for defect density correlation; extension to multiple TMD heterostructure systems.

high_risk_ideas.expected_mechanism: If rotational relaxation proceeds via nucleation and growth of commensurate domains, the competition between domain nucleation rate and growth rate (limited by interfacial phonon drag at high T) will produce a TTT nose curve. high_risk_ideas.discriminating_observation: The stability phase diagram must exhibit a nose curve shape, distinguishing it from simple Arrhenius relaxation. high_risk_ideas.boundary_or_failure_condition: The TTT stability framework fails if: (1) relaxation follows simple monotonic Arrhenius kinetics without a nose curve; (2) thermal conductivity changes do not correlate with moiré periodicity models; (3) relaxation is dominated by uniform sliding rather than domain nucleation and growth; (4) the framework does not transfer to other TMD combinations.

high_risk_ideas.falsifier: Observation of simple monotonic Arrhenius relaxation kinetics without a nose curve, or lack of correlation between thermal conductivity changes and moiré superlattice phonon scattering models.

evaluation.fairness_protocol: The proposal uses Raman spectroscopy before and after annealing to decouple defect density changes from twist angle contributions, and compares the TTT model against pre-registered competing kinetic models (Avrami, threshold, monotonic) to ensure fair evaluation of the mechanism.
evaluation.feedback: The proposal successfully replaces the implicit stability assumption with an explicit, quantifiable mechanism (interfacial rotational relaxation) and introduces a rigorous temperature-time matrix isolation protocol. Additionally, clarify how the initial twist angle distribution (0-5 degrees) might affect the kinetics, as larger initial angles could introduce different relaxation pathways or strain fields.
